Supports custom cache names for scan_uni2, with three variants for vision cache: standard, freq, staig_strict. 🔄 Verification of M14 Baseline Evaluation Infrastructure and Full Assessment Start (2026-02-22) — Sanity check (60 episodes, ~7 minutes, SR=0% as expected), followed by start of full CPU assessment for 649 scenarios × 2 strategies × 3 seeds (≈ 3894 episodes), running in the background. 🔄 Construction of Full Data Pipeline for Phoenix pi0.5 Reproduction (2026-02-22) — Written convert_mimicgen_to_lerobot.py and evaluate_mimicgen.py, configured pi05_base_mimicgen_phoenix training parameters, downloaded the 18.4GB MimicGen dataset via hf-mirror.com (9 tasks, 9000 demos), and completed format conversion (7–8/9 tasks). 🔄 Joint Evaluation of SCAN Embedding and Multimodal Fusion (2026-02-19) — Written eval_scan_fusion.py, comparing the optimized 256-dimensional visual embedding of SCAN with PCA gene features across all fusion methods; mean fusion achieved ARI +0.065, partially resolved the coords dimension bug, and script debugging in progress. 🔄 Implementation and Batch Experiments of MIHD Vision Refinement Two-Stage Fusion Framework (2026-02-22) — Added –vision_refine parameter (scan_cluster/stego_refine/byol_spatial), with ~60 lines of code minimal intrusion, first experiment showed ARI=0.313 lower than baseline concat 0.387; 7 fusion strategies running in the background. ✅ Completion of Full Phase II Execution Plan for Error Recovery Benchmark (2026-02-22) — Analyzed the dependencies between large goals G1–G7 and milestones M12–M15, developed a 7-step execution plan, and clarified the GPU allocation strategy (srun –overlap, ≥50% free memory), with a key path of approximately 16 days. ✅ Diagnosis of Error Recovery Benchmark Baseline and Update of GPU Access Specification (2026-02-22) — Resolved Pi0.5 OOM (150MB memory shortage), BC-RNN obs key issue, and 649 scenario readiness; standardized GPU access in CLAUDE.md and MEMORY.md to srun –overlap. 🚫 Extension of force parameters in visualize_scene.py (2026-02-22) — Completed addition of force_override/duration_override/settle_steps parameters and Phase 3 neutral action logic; video validation blocked due to SLURM node permissions issues. ✅ Special Comparative Experiment for STAIG Fusion (151673) (2026-02-20) — Tested staig_fusion × {UNI2_raw, SCAN(UNI2)} separately, ARI values were 0.3929/0.3880, almost equal; verified that STAIG internal StandardScaler+PCA offset the effects of SCAN optimization. ✅ Addition of H&E Panel and Batch Update of UNI2 Visualization (2026-02-19) — Changed to a 1×3 layout (H&E + GT + prediction), re-generated all 11 sections visually using .npz cache, 151510 fixed via hires→lowres symlink. Issues and Solutions 1. STEGO Training loss is NaN throughout, 3639×3639 dense similarity matrix overflows in float32 operations at temperature=0.07 [MIHD] (2026-02-19) Solution: Two-step fix: perform L2 normalization on the input image_emb;Change InfoNCE to the numerical stability version (subtract the maximum value of rows before computing logsumexp, and increase temperature to 0.1).
2. MILWRM was incorrectly classified as an Image-Only method; the initial AI summary will mix multimodal methods with image-only results. The initial research conclusion needs significant revision [MIHD] (2026-02-19)Solution: Use WebFetch to read the full PMC text and confirm that MILWRM is actually based on gene expression, specifically mining only image-only data points from ablation experiments on articles like SpaConTDS. 3. There is a double normalization bug in staig_fusion in eval_scan_fusion.py (STAIGTrainer internally applies StandardScaler again) [MIHD] (2026-02-20) Solution: Abandon fixing the standalone script and directly use run_benchmark.py that correctly passes staig_alignment_config, reusing the verified path.
4. run_benchmark.py instantiates the encoder each time to extract embeddings, lacking pipeline-level cache support [MIHD] (2026-02-20) Solution: Integrate CacheManager from pipeline/cache_manager.py, load from cache before encoding, and write back to cache after extraction; skip encoder instantiation when a cache hit occurs.
5. Lerobot 0.1.0 is incompatible with datasets >=4.0 (torch.stack reports TypeError: Column object replaces list) [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Downgrade datasets from 4.4.1 to 3.6.0 (<4.0); datasets 4.0 changes the return value of dataset[‘column’] from a list to a Column object, and Lerobot expects a list/tuple of tensors.
6. The official HuggingFace download fails due to proxy (Squid 503), and the Python download script cannot connect [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Use hf-mirror.com + wget; URL format: https://hf-mirror.com/datasets/{repo_id}/resolve/main/{file_path}，通过集群 HTTP proxy reaches 40–200MB/s.
7. Unstable access to SLurm GPU nodes: srun lacks –overlap, causing command hangs; direct SSH connection is unreliable, and multi-partition submissions are rejected [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Standardize the workflow: source set-XY-I.sh → squeue → srun –jobid= –overlap; avoid direct SSH to GPU nodes.
8. Abnormal spatial coordinate dimension in eval_scan_fusion.py (turns into (1,2)), causing errors in multiple fusion methods [MIHD] (2026-02-19) Solution: Abandon calling load_spatial_coordinates() (barcode matching fails), and directly read coordinates from adata.obsm[‘spatial’]; fix the unpacking error in load_dlpfc_data return value.
Learning Gains Domain Knowledge (domain) Pure image-only achieves only 0.11–0.16 ARI in DLPFC fine-grained stratification tasks (multimodal reaches 0.45–0.64), which is a combination of extremely small morphological differences between brain layers and mismatch in the Foundation Model training domain; ablation experiments of multimodal methods almost never test image-only separately—this is a noteworthy research gap. Five main reasons for failure in space domain recognition by Foundation Models: ① Training mainly on cancer tissue (domain gap); ② Pre-training task mismatch with inter-layer gradient recognition; ③ Extremely small morphological differences between cerebral cortex layers; ④ High redundancy between image features and gene expression; ⑤ Lack of spatial context in independent encoding of a single patch. STAIG uses BYOL for unsupervised domain adaptation on target dataset H&E patches (keep encoder after training, discard projector/predictor)—this is a direct precedent for introducing unsupervised domain adaptation into spatial transcriptomics; the design of BYOL without negative samples is naturally suitable for small batch ST scenarios (thousands of patches per section). The CV community has a four-stage framework for handling “domain gap + fine-grained task + unlabeled data”: Level 1: direct pre-trained feature clustering → Level 2: STEGO/SCAN feature refinement → Level 3: domain-specific SSL re-training (BYOL/MAE) → Level 4: dedicated Foundation Model; GPFM/CHIEF are the optimal PFM for space domain recognition ARI, and UNI2 are the optimal spot retrieval. Architecture (architecture) SCAN is the optimal ARI (0.303, +20.6%) in image-only spatial transcriptomics scenarios. Its core advantage is that offline feature k-NN mining decouples embedding learning and clustering; its 256-dimensional optimized embeddings complement gene features (mean fusion +0.065 ARI). Two-stage fusion is not necessarily better than single-stage: after scanning_cluster compresses visual embeddings from 1536d to 256d, multimodal fusion ARI (0.313) is lower than direct concat (0.387), indicating that self-supervised compression loses the original feature diversity required for fusion tasks, and the optimization objectives of self-supervised clustering conflict with downstream fusion tasks. Internal StandardScaler+PCA preprocessing in STAIG fusion absorbs the external embedding optimization effect (the ARI difference between SCAN and UNI2_raw is only 0.005); embedding cache should store raw embeddings before normalization, and post-encoder normalization should be performed after loading to ensure consistent results across different call paths. VLA baseline evaluation must explicitly state the checkpoint source: using non-target task fine-tuning models (pi0_libero, pi05_base) to evaluate zero-sample cross-domain recovery capacity—the paper must actively declare this experimental setup, and subsequent comparative experiments after fine-tuning are needed to fully demonstrate the usefulness of the dataset. In complex experimental systems, prefer using existing, verified tool paths (such as run_benchmark.py); standalone scripts easily introduce hidden bugs such as inconsistent preprocessing; before calling internal project functions, read the source code in real time to verify the function signature, rather than relying on memory. Debugging (debugging) When computing large-scale dense similarity matrix (n>3000) and InfoNCE contrast loss, use numerically stable log-sum-exp (subtracting row maximum), otherwise exponential operations with temperature=0.07 at float32 precision will overflow and produce NaN; this is a key engineering constraint for large-scale contrast learning implementation. Tools (tools) Lerobot 0.1.0 has strict constraints on datasets versions; it must be pinned to <4.0 (recommended 3.x); datasets 4.0 change the return value of dataset[‘column’] to a Column object, causing torch.stack to report TypeError; MimicGen is fully compatible with LIBERO obs/action format (84×84 images, 8D state, 7D action)—OpenPI’s LeRobotLiberoDataConfig can be directly reused. The standard solution for accessing HuggingFace on Chinese mainland HPC clusters is hf-mirror.com; URL format: https://hf-mirror.com/datasets/{repo_id}/resolve/main/{file_path}，通过 wget + HTTP proxy reaches 40–200MB/s—this should be used as the default solution. OpenPI’s JAX training naturally supports multi-GPU data parallelism; just specify the GPU list in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and JAX automatically builds a 2D mesh parallel—no changes to TrainConfig are needed; Slurm –overlap is a key parameter for running new commands on existing interactive jobs—it is a core technique for calling cluster GPUs in Claude Code environment. AI Usage Notes Effective Modes:
✓ Parallel sub-tasks explore the project structure and formulate cleanup plans (MIHD organizes tasks), reducing serial exploration time. ✓ Parallel background execution on GPU with three schemes (STEGO/BYOL/SCAN) for comparison and validation, significantly reducing total experimental time. ✓ Use .npz caching to generate visualizations in bulk, completely decoupling inference and visualization—11/11 sections succeed. ✓ Independent temporary script (_test_staig_scan.py) isolates testing a single fusion method, shortening a 2-hour task to 30 seconds. ✓ Independent exploration of JAX multi-GPU mechanisms (no config changes) and the hf-mirror.com alternative download method—no user intervention required. ✓ Minimal invasive code change (about 60 lines): insert a Vision Refinement stage in run_benchmark.py, maintaining architecture stability. Limitations:
✗ Inadequate accuracy in literature classification: MILWRM is incorrectly classified as image-only method; initial research aggregation mixes with multimodal results—requires two user interventions to converge on the correct research boundary. ✗ Lack of awareness to actively expose key experimental assumptions: No explicit mention of the impact of using LIBERO fine-tuning checkpoint in VLA evaluation on experiment effectiveness—needs user inquiry to discuss further. ✗ API usage tends to rely on memory rather than real-time verification: Multiple function signature/return value unpacking errors occur in eval_scan_fusion.py—source code should be read before calling. ✗ Slurm permission issues tend to involve listing multiple partitions (5+ times)—no quick query to the user about correct account/partition information. ✗ Insufficient status judgment for background tasks: Data conversion is still running when LeRobot dataset validation triggers, leading to false timestamp violation errors; frequent sleep polling is interrupted multiple times. ✗ Using CPU by default for model validation in HPC environments hides real performance issues, causing additional interaction overhead. Next Week’s Plan Next week will focus on three parallel lines: ①MIHD: fix the coordinate bug in eval_scan_fusion.py, complete joint evaluation of SCAN embedding and full fusion strategies, analyze batch results of 7 fusion strategies and diagnose the root cause of Vision Refinement compression losses, and consider adjusting refinement hidden_dim or switching to stego_refine/byol_spatial; ②Error Recovery Benchmark: organize full CPU evaluation results for M14 649 scenario, solve Pi0.5 OOM problem (apply larger memory GPU or reduce batch size), start Phoenix pi0.5 100K steps 4-GPU training; ③Engineering blocking removal: resolve SLURM node permission issues and complete visualize_scene.py video validation, resolve Pi0 VLA Server port conflict (detect with lsof -i:5555 + backup port mechanism), and advance implementation of ImageEncoder enhancement for goal 7 in ENHANCEMENT_PLAN_CN.md.

Key Insight: When evaluating models using built-in feature alignment or normalization layers, the external preprocessing process must pass a clear override flag or completely skip normalization to avoid signal distortion.

Key Insight: The policy inference process must strictly maintain the original observation pattern during expansion, as internal state extractors often lose or compress keys required by pre-trained adapters.
General Issues 4. Failure of MimicGen data set generation in RoboMimic 0.3.0 is due to passing outdated kwargs to create_env_for_data_processing, causing environment instantiation crashes. Solution: Dynamically checked the real-time API signature, updated the wrapper to pass only supported parameters conditionally, and automatically fallback when expected fields are missing from environment metadata.
Key Insight: Version locking of third-party ML environments is crucial; dynamic signature checks or strict version restrictions can prevent hidden API damage during data flow execution.

Problems and Solutions Key Problems 1. Pre-trained pathological base models exhibit severe distribution shifts in fine cortical layer recognition and clustering anatomy due to surgical-oriented pre-training and subtle morphological gradients, causing these regions to be artificially distorted. Solution: Abandoned the original frozen encoder clustering and adopted target-domain self-supervised adaptation strategies (such as STEGO feature matching蒸馏, BYOL potential guidance), combined with on-the-fly optimization. Key insight: The base model optimized for coarse organizational phenotypes lacks the micro-scale spatial gradient retention required for fine domain transformation; unsupervised clustering alone cannot verify cross-modal alignment and requires specific domain-target adjustments.
2. InfoNCE loss converges to NaN, and downstream fusion methods crash due to dense similarity matrix overflow, float32 precision limitations, and shape mismatches in old coordinate loaders. Solution: Applied sklearn L2 normalization pre-projection, limited similarity to float64 tensors, repaired the data loader to extract coordinates directly from adata.obsm, and replaced inline shell commands with independent execution scripts with cache bypass flags.
Key insight: Contrast targets with wide spatial neighborhoods require strict numerical stability protocols; redundant coordinate acquisition introduces dimensional mismatch and disrupts the unified evaluation scheduling mechanism.
3. Distributed benchmark tests lasting 15 hours are highly susceptible to node timeout, crashes, and environmental failures, lacking an automatic recovery mechanism or consistent OS-specific configurations. Solution: Integrated episode-based recovery mechanisms in the collector, skipped completed tuples; implemented offset/limited CLI slicing for fault-tolerant sub-batch processing; disabled Windows OpenSSH ControlMaster multiplexing to clear outdated sockets; aligned GPU device environment variables.
Key insight: HPC workflows require explicit state recovery mechanisms rather than external checkpoints; cross-platform development networks need strict parameter auditing to prevent implicit hardware degradation or persistent connection failures.
General Problems 4. Iterative document updates lead to information accumulation and redundant architectural descriptions, causing large markdown files to exceed the context window during roadmap planning. Solution: Applied block-based automated refactoring, retained all operational milestone hierarchies, used pattern matching for targeted structural editing, and verified completeness via Grep before final submission.
Key insight: Appendive document updates inevitably separate from infrastructure realities; strategic compression must balance information density with organizational tracking needs to maintain long-term agent introduction efficiency.

AI Limitations It is difficult to directly access the full academic paywall, and it is hard to distinguish independent single-modal benchmarks from multimodal ablation studies, requiring repeated fallback queries and strict user constraint filtering to separate pure morphological performance metrics. The limited autonomous environment perception leads to initial CPU usage despite GPU requirements, and visual artifacts are misattributed to incorrect model sources until precise Slurm strategy context is obtained through operational feedback. Context window limitations force manual segmentation of large repository documents during roadmap updates, and automatic code generation occasionally produces Shell escape conflicts or numpy boolean patterns that violate existing project norms. Lessons Learned Key Lessons Learned Pure visual spatial clustering yields low ARI (~0.1–0.2); morphological features alone cannot capture cortical details, so multimodal fusion or target-specific self-supervised alignment is mathematically necessary for effective domain transformation. Dense contrast targets and long-term distributed evaluation require strict input L2 normalization, float64 precision buffering, explicit cache bypass flags, and episode-based recovery logic to prevent gradient explosion, stale reads, and state loss. Practical Lessons — In abstract planning, human participation in coordinating loop terminology is crucial; clear constraints on experimental scope and validation standards avoid structurally reasonable but practically mismatched workflows, while block document refactoring must preserve organizational hierarchy while pursuing syntactic simplicity. Subsequent work integrates self-supervised strategies (STEGO, BYOL+GAT, SCAN) into the MIHD process, and issues related to InfoNCE differences are resolved through L2 normalization and precision constraints. Parallel benchmark tests on spatial transcriptomics data show that compared to frozen encoders, SCAN processed features have a significant advantage over PCA gene embedding, and the visualization process has been updated to include high-resolution H&E reference panels for direct morphological correlation analysis.

Phase II planning integrates G1-G4 goals into a 16-day execution roadmap, prioritizing manual remote operation recovery data and strict baseline tests (random/BC-RNN/Pi0). Log export (data correction) was successful, but downstream report generation was hindered due to the unavailable LLM API. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. The single-modal ARI of MIHD visual encoder is extremely low (approximately 0.065), which does not match historical UNI2 performance; the embedding vectors show abnormal patterns (initially many duplicate rows). Solution: An in-depth investigation of tissue_positions_list.csv revealed that col4 corresponds to pxl_row_in_fullres (Y-axis) rather than pixel_x, and col5 corresponds to pxl_col_in_fullres (X-axis) rather than pixel_y, although the code naming is reversed. By analyzing the step changes of array_row/array_col, it was confirmed that col4 changes by 119.8px per step (Y-axis), and col5 changes by 68.9px per step (X-axis). The column name was corrected to (pxl_col, pxl_row) to resolve this.Key Findings: Data errors are more subtle than model errors: the code runs normally, caching is generated successfully, and tests pass, but all results are based on incorrect data. We need to trace anomalies at the macro level (low ARI) back to the original data source (CSV column definitions). The Euclidean invariance of spatial distance means graph construction is unaffected, but the visual patch content is completely misplaced.
2. ccusage returns cost=0 for Claude-opus-4-6, causing severe token cost tracking failure (actual $43 on February 17 shows $0.90, which is 13 times underestimated) Solution: A backup pricing mechanism was implemented in the fetch_ccusage() function of daily_summary.py through post-processing logic _fix_zero_cost_models(). A dictionary _FALLBACK_PRICING was added (opus-4-6: input $5/model, output $25/model, caching creation $6.25/model, caching reading $0.50/model) to calculate correct costs. Field name errors were fixed (mb.get(‘model’) → mb.get(‘modelName’) or mb.get(‘model’)) to ensure compatibility. Logs for February 13–17 were re-exported, and the displayed costs were corrected from $3–7 per day to actual $18–48 per day.
Key Findings: Defects in third-party tool pricing cannot be directly fixed—a local backup mechanism is used as a practical solution. LiteLLM uses versioned model names (anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1 with -v1 suffix), while Claude Code logs use simplified names (claude-opus-4-6), leading to systematic mismatches. The backup design must trigger only when anomalies occur (cost=0) to maintain backward compatibility when upstream fixes appear. Cost tracking errors can lead to over 90% underestimation (13 times in this case), severely affecting resource planning decisions. Always verify the output format of third-party tools by printing the original data rather than inferring from documents.
3. The Tianhe non-pulse injector (friction/pose perturbation/gripping bias) crashes when trying to parse body/geometry IDs in the MuJoCo model due to “AttributeError: no attribute mj_name2id” Solution: The model.body_name2id() and model.geom_name2id() methods are wrapped by robosuite instead of direct mujoco.mj_name2id(). An auxiliary function _resolve_body_id() is added, first trying “name” then trying “name_main” suffix (robosuite naming convention). The try/except mechanism is used to handle missing bodies gracefully.
Key Findings: Robosuite wraps MuJoCo through its own API layer and adds a _main suffix after the object name. Direct calls to MuJoCo C API bypass the framework layer and cause crashes—only the wrapping function provided by the framework must be used for name conversion. The robot simulation framework layer abstracts the original physics engine; direct API calls bypassing the framework cause crashes. Before modification, always check valid reference code in the same codebase (e.g., ImpulseInjector) for the same code library.
4. The Tianhe BC-RNN strategy crashes due to KeyError 'object' because the obs dictionary generated by StateExtractor contains the key ‘object-state’, while robomimic training data uses the key ‘object’ (different robosuite tasks have inconsistent key names: PickPlace uses object-state, Lift uses object) Solution: A key mapping was added in _to_robosuite_obs() Strategy 1, converting the object-state alias into object before returning the original obs. The backup solution for Strategy 3 was updated, merging objects from StateExtractor into a object key using pos + quat. Verified by 79 unit tests and GPU integration tests—KeyError has been eliminated.
Key Findings: Robosuite automatically adds a -state suffix after grouping modalities (e.g., object → object-state), but training data uses the original names. The adapter layer must fill this naming convention gap. Different robosuite tasks have inconsistent observation key naming rules. Manual reconstruction of obs cannot guarantee consistency with key names during training. The safest approach is to directly pass the original env.step() return value via a key alias. This indicates that cross-task compatibility requires either (a) a unified obs format or (b) a clear key mapping layer.
5. LLMs often return corrupted JSON in structured reports: unescaped quotes, incomplete objects, extra text, or truncation near token limits, leading to parsing failures and workflow interruptionsSolution: A four-stage backup parser was implemented: (1) directly use json.loads(), (2) extract json blocks, (3) find a complete JSON object based on deep matching of bracket structures, (4) call the LLM to fix the corrupted JSON. For APIs that support this feature, use tool_use (Anthropic) or response_format=json_object (OpenAI) to force valid JSON. Key Insight: Structured data generated by LLMs require multiple backup strategies for defensive parsing. The native JSON mode (tool_use/json_object) can significantly reduce errors, but cannot completely avoid failures. Using the LLM fix as the final backup solution can build a robust process. Each backup layer handles a specific type of failure: code blocks handle Markdown formatting, bracket matching handles truncation issues, and the fix handles syntax errors.
6. The BC-RNN model has a 0% success rate after resolving KeyError—the robot hovers over the box but cannot approach the target Solution: Three visual videos (400 frames each) were generated to show the robot’s behavior. The root cause was identified as a training insufficient checkpoint (epoch 600, limited demo data), not a framework bug. The video shows the robot hovers but never tries to grab. More training epochs or better checkpoints are needed.
Key Insight: Even if unit tests pass, GPU integration tests are crucial. BC-RNN passed all 79 unit tests, but actual operation on GPU reveals 0% SR issues. Video visualization is important for diagnosing behavioral quality issues in robots. Framework correctness and model quality require different verification strategies: unit tests/integration tests confirm code logic; video visualization reveals behavior quality.
7. SSH connections to the Tianhe HPC cluster often disconnect, causing Claude Code sessions to be lost and work to fail; VS Code Remote SSH is also affected Solution: A multi-layer deep defense scheme was implemented: (1) set up SSH keep-alive on both ends (15-second heartbeat, 90-second tolerance), (2) use tmux sessions for persistence so processes continue after disconnection, (3) write Claude-tmux scripts to restore sessions with one-click via automatic proxy, (4) comment out the automatic proxy in .bashrc to isolate the user environment from shared accounts, (5) write local client configuration instructions for ControlMaster multiplexing and automatic SSH reconnection scripts.
Key Insight: Network instability requires multiple layers of redundancy: protocol layer (TCP keep-alive), SSH layer (ControlMaster), application layer (tmux + automatic reconnection). No single layer is sufficient to ensure production environment reliability. tmux separates session state from connection status, achieving true recovery capability. Session-level proxy configuration (not global .bashrc) avoids affecting other shared account users. When working on shared server accounts, each environment modification (PATH, proxy, alias) must consider multi-user impacts.
8. The multi-device daily report workflow requires a synchronization mechanism—device-independent exports but merged reports require access to all device exports, and merged devices may not have access to these files Solution: A two-layer rclone synchronization is used: export files are uploaded to <remote>/logs/, merged reports are uploaded to <remote>/reports/. The merge --sync flag is added before LLM aggregation to download logs/files from all devices. A _merged_devices tracking mechanism is implemented to avoid re-summarizing already processed devices.
Key Insight: Distributed workflows require clear synchronization points. Separating original export files (logs/) from aggregated output (reports/) prevents circular dependencies. Idempotent design (skipping processed content) can be safely run again without expensive redundant API calls.
9. The original single-device daily report design assumes a single device; when users need multi-device aggregation, the current architecture cannot handle it Solution: The single-stage design (reading dialogue → calling API → generating report) was completely refactored into a two-stage design (Stage 1: export dialogue as JSON per device; Stage 2: merge all exports and call API to generate a summary report). This architectural change was explicitly requested by users.
Key Insight: User requirements change during development. Human users discovered the single-device limitation, while AI did not anticipate it in the initial design. The two-stage architecture is more complex but necessary for real-world use cases. This indicates that human system thinking is superior at anticipating distributed deployment limitations.
10. Scene generation produced zero-friction/gripping bias scenes, despite the injector being enabled (initially only pose_perturb was effective) Solution: The detector only generates specific sub-types of friction/gripping bias ErrorSpecs, which do not trigger during operation. A _augment_specs_with_alternatives() method was implemented to programmatically generate friction/gripping and clamping bias/scrambled specifications when the original detector yields no results. 100 additional friction scenes were generated (55 scrambled, 28 tip overshoot, 17 large offsets), expanding the database to 454 scenes.
Key Insight: Error scene generation is a funnel: detector triggers → ErrorSpec generation → injector application → validation → scene acceptance. Enabling the injector does not guarantee generated scenes—it depends on the frequency of detector triggers. Different error types have distinct acceptance rates depending on the task. In pick-and-place tasks, pose perturbation is more generalizable than friction/gripping anomalies. Programmatic specifications can compensate for the coverage gap of the detector.
11. No MimicGen pre-trained BC-RNN checkpoints are available for PickPlace tasks Solution: A comprehensive search (official repository, HuggingFace, local filesystem) confirmed that MimicGen only provides datasets and not pre-trained model weights. The demo dataset generated by MimicGen is used to design self-training plans via the robomimic framework.
Key Insight: Official releases may provide data but not trained models. Always verify resource availability before planning dependent workflows. When pre-trained checkpoints are unavailable, training from demonstrations becomes a necessary backup solution.
General Issues 12. Model checkpoints are scattered across the filesystem (BC-RNN under tangzijia/, VLA models under zhaoganlong/, total size 47GB), hindering management and reproducibility Solution: Design checkpoints/directories and use symbolic links to avoid duplication: bc_rnn/pick_place → original path, vla/{pi0_libero, pi05_base, pi0_base, pi0_fast_base} → zhaoganlong cache. Updated benchmark_v4.yaml to use the new centralized path.
Key Insight: Large model assets (47GB+ VLA checkpoints) require a symbolic link-based organization to avoid duplication while maintaining centralized discoverability. Scattered checkpoints in the filesystem hinder reproducibility and configuration management.
13. Hugo preamble generation uses hard-coded “AI Daily Summary” and incorrect time zone (+08:00 instead of -05:00), inconsistent with existing bugJournal entries Solution: Adjust the preamble generation to use the correct time zone (-05:00). Solution: The generate_hugo_post() function was modified to extract the actual summary from the double-quote region (line 3, starting with ‘>’) in the report; the time zone was changed to -05:00; time was set to T00:00:00; the “AI Daily Summary” keyword was removed from the keywords.
Key Insight: Code generation should follow existing content standards rather than imposing new ones. Reading the actual report structure (double-quote summary) is easier to maintain than hard-coded strings.

Multiple failed exit plan mode attempts indicated difficulty in judging whether the plan optimization was complete and whether users wanted further iteration. The AI rejected the plan three times across different sessions, indicating that “is this plan ready?” should be asked instead of assuming it was completed. - It was impossible to directly analyze video content to evaluate strategy quality. BC-RNN promotion videos required manual extraction of key frames and manual inspection to identify robot hovering behavior (ignoring grasping targets). Without visual confirmation, a 0% success rate could not be inferred, indicating quality issues with the model. - When API ConnectionRefused errors occurred during report generation, no alternative solution was proposed (data was fully corrected first, then report generation was processed separately). The flexibility of workflow decoupling was insufficient. - A long unified plan document containing server-side and local client instructions was created, but execution boundaries were not considered. User feedback was needed to reconstruct it into executable results. The project decomposition ability was weak. - When the user asked in Chinese “Where are we now?”, the exploration agent was activated and read a large amount of documentation, instead of checking the recent session context or TODO tracking system first. Excessive reliance on file reading was needed, while conversation context might be sufficient. ## Lessons learned ### Key lessons – Data errors are more hidden and destructive than model errors: MIHD coordinate exchange errors caused all visual experiment results to fail, but the code logic was completely normal and all tests passed. Issues need to be investigated from macro-level metric anomalies (ARI) back to data sources (CSV column definitions). This requires a complete data scientist thought chain; unit tests alone cannot detect such errors. - Name convention differences in cross-framework integration are hidden traps: the `_main` suffix in robosuite, differences in observation key names for different tasks (object and object state), and the `-v1` suffix in LiteLLM—these details are not obvious in the documentation but cause runtime errors. The robot simulation framework covers the original physics engine through layer abstraction (robosuite encapsulates MuJoCo). Direct API calls bypassing the framework layers cause problems—framework wrappers must be used to handle naming conventions (such as `_main` suffix) and state management. Robosuite observation key naming rule: the environment automatically adds `-state` suffix after grouping mode (e.g., `object` → `object-state`), but training data usually uses the original names. The adapter layer must handle this mismatch. The safest strategy is: (1) use the framework-wrapped API instead of the underlying API; (2) use the original data structure instead of manual reconstruction; (3) print actual output to verify field names, rather than relying on documentation. Check the available reference code in the same codebase before modification. - Framework correctness and model quality require different validation strategies. Unit tests/integration tests can confirm code logic and eliminate KeyError and other errors. Video visualization can reveal behavior quality issues (robot hovering and grasping). Even if unit tests pass, GPU integration tests are crucial—BC-RNN passed 79 unit tests, but 0% SR problems and under-trained checkpoints could only be detected through GPU deployment and visualization checks. Each validation layer has a different role. - The multi-device collaborative daily report tool establishes a closed loop: each device exports local logs → the central node merges remote logs → unified deployment to Hugo → publishing to GitHub Pages. This process was used extensively on 2026-02-17 (processing 4 historical dates), proving the feasibility of the two-stage architecture. The next step is automation (proposed by users but not implemented). Meta-tools (used to analyze tool usage) require careful consideration of workflow allocation—conditions on each device, data synchronization methods, and partial information processing methods. The two-stage architecture (local export + centralized aggregation) is more suitable for distributed scenarios than a single monolithic stage design. - The expansion from 251 to 454 of the error recovery benchmark scenario library is a successful case of incremental expansion: first implementing the pulse injector (M4) → discovering the need for non-pulse types (M5) → fixing MuJoCo API compatibility → generating multiple type scenarios through the detector candidate extension mechanism. This shows an iterative path from the minimum viable product to fully functional features. Error scenario generation is a funnel: detector triggers → error specification generation → injector application → validation → scenario acceptance. Enabling injectors does not guarantee generated scenarios—it depends on the trigger frequency of detectors. Acceptance rates for different error types vary greatly depending on task dynamics. Pose perturbation is more common in pick-and-place tasks than friction/grasping anomalies. Programmatic spec augmentation (_augment_specs_with_alternatives()) can compensate for insufficient detector coverage. - Defensive programming is required for third-party tool integration: zero-cost patches (ccusage), field name compatibility (modelName or model), and self-degradable mechanisms designed for future fixes (when LiteLLM fixes occur, fallback becomes no operation). This “activate only when needed” patch strategy minimizes maintenance costs. Pricing issues of third-party tools should be resolved through local fallback mechanisms rather than waiting for upstream fixes. Design fallback should only trigger in abnormal values (cost = 0) to ensure backward compatibility. LiteLLM uses versioned model names (anthropic.{model}-v1 with an optional:0 suffix), while Claude Code logs use simplified names, leading to systematic mismatches. Cost tracking errors may cause over-underestimation by more than 90% (13 observations), severely affecting financial planning. Regular audits of cost metrics are crucial. - When human-machine collaboration is optimal, humans specify the system architecture and strategic decisions, and the AI is responsible for technical implementation and optimization. In this meeting, users’ architectural insights (two-stage design, multi-device synchronization) were important; the AI’s technical execution capabilities (parsing alternative solutions, configuration optimization) filled the gaps. Qualitative judgments from domain experts are crucial for identifying systematic issues. Data-driven analysis by AI and human intuition form an effective complement. - Remote development in unstable connection environments requires multiple layers of defense: maintaining active connections (prevention), session persistence (handling interruptions), multiple connections (quick reconnection), and automated scripts (resumption). Single-layer solutions will fail in real network environments. For shared server accounts, user-specific custom settings should be placed in conditional blocks or independent startup scripts, rather than affecting all users’ common .bashrc configuration. tmux simultaneously handles state persistence and environment boundaries. Proxy configurations for session scope (not global bashrc) can avoid affecting other shared account users. - Structured data generated by LLMs require multiple alternative parsing strategies for protection. The native JSON pattern (Anthropic uses tool_use, OpenAI uses json_object) helps somewhat, but failures cannot be completely avoided—fixing is always the last resort. Each alternative layer targets specific failure modes: code blocks handle Markdown formatting, bracket matching handles truncation issues, and repair functions handle syntax errors. - The daily summary tool can benefit from gradual architecture evolution: starting with a simple task/problem list, adding session summaries to provide context, and adding priority metadata for filtering. Each layer meets the needs of different readers. Batch document workflows benefit from the two-stage architecture: (1) extraction of source files based on local context; (2) integration across sources and global deduplication. This pattern also appears in summary tools (export → merge), MIHD processes (first stage cache embedding → second stage fusion), and error recovery tests (generate scenarios → collect data). - MimicGen release policy: only datasets are provided, no pre-trained model checkpoints. The official version may only provide data without the trained model—confirm resource availability before planning. BC-RNN (with RNN behavior cloning) is a simple supervised learning method: collect human demonstration (state, behavior) pairs, train LSTM to predict behavior, and then deploy as a strategy. When enough demonstrations are available, this is a simple and effective foundation for handling manipulation tasks. When pre-trained checkpoints are unavailable, training from demonstrations becomes a necessary backup. - Post-work log analysis (summarizing the past week’s work) is a valuable practice; it converts raw conversation logs into structured knowledge outcomes, helping identify patterns and track progress over long periods—powerful design patterns for idempotency (tracking processed content, avoiding duplicate work) are crucial for processes that may be interrupted or restarted. The _merged_devices tracking mechanism avoids expensive duplicate API calls when processing partially completed aggregated data. - Large model asset management (47GB+ VLA checkpoints) requires an organizational approach based on symbolic links to avoid duplication while maintaining centralized discoverability. Dispersed checkpoints in the file system hinder reproducibility and configuration management. A centralized checkpoint directory improves discoverability. - When fixing historical data quality errors, separating data correction (export) from downstream consumption (report generation) is important. This avoids entire process interruptions due to downstream dependency failures (e.g., LLM API unavailable). The export stage depends on Node.js tools (ccusage), and the merging stage depends on the LLM API—even if merging is blocked, export can continue. ### Practical experience summary - The scope of complex research project documents should not only cover main modules but also include dependencies/submodules (11 in the Motion framework), data transformation pipelines, and integration points across repositories (LeRobot, OpenPI, MimicGen). Thorough exploration can prevent incomplete documents from causing onboarding difficulties. ## Conversation summary ### MIHD **🔄 Fix visual encoder X/Y coordinate exchange errors and prepare to run experiments again** _18:50:27.298 | claude_code_ The user found abnormal UNI2 clustering results (151670 has only one cluster, ARI≈0.065). Deep debugging revealed two serious issues: (1) coordinate space mismatch (high resolution vs full resolution), and (2) X/Y coordinate exchange (CSV column 4=Y/column 5=X, but code naming is opposite). The root cause was confirmed by analyzing the relationship between array_row/array_col and pixel coordinates. load_spatial_coordinates() and VisionEncoder coordinate processing logic were fixed, and an execution plan for running 66 single-modal experiments (3 gene encoders + 3 visual encoders × 11 partial tasks) was written, but the user interrupted it when entering the exit plan mode.**🔄 Fully fixed coordinate errors and verified through re-run via experiments** _21:28:38.729 | claude_code_ Fixed the CSV column mapping error in load_spatial_coordinates() (pixel_x is actually Y/pxl_row, pixel_y is X/pxl_col), causing all visual patches to be extracted from transposed positions, with a visual ARI of only 0.065. The column names and coordinate order in scripts/run_benchmark.py and utils/data_loader.py were modified, all spatial_coords and visual caches were cleaned up, and the embeddings for 11 parts of UNI2/HIPT/ResNet50 were re-extracted. Verified that the coordinates are correct and the embeddings are 100% unique, with the UNI2 ARI increased to 0.12-0.25. The core multimodal fast fusion experiment was restarted (STAIG UNI extraction completed, evaluation in progress). ### gadget-summarize **✅ Generated a report for 4 devices on 2026-02-13** _13:56:41.357 | claude_code_ Large-scale integration of work on 2026-02-13, involving DCC (MIHD 286-experiment benchmark automation), tianhe (error recovery code cleanup v4.0→v4.1, GPU smoke test), MacBook (creating a daily report tool using a two-stage architecture), and Windows (CalendarPro P0 fix). Implementation Methods: Coordinated parallel GPU validation tasks, refactored observation/state extraction mapping under simulation strategies, reviewed code library and documentation consistency, and implemented a configuration-based synchronization mechanism. DCC Completed Tasks: Conducted MIHD benchmark tests, reviewed architecture documentation, and extended the daily summary CLI. Implementation Methods: Used Claude Code’s file system/network tools for environment isolation, symbolic link routing, and parallel configuration validation. Impact: Verified performance baselines of fusion strategies, standardized project milestone tracking, and implemented reliable head-to-desktop log aggregation. TzJsDesktop Completed Tasks: Performed strategic architecture planning, v4.5 pipeline planning, and design of human-readable report formats. Implementation Methods: Linked implementation progress with roadmap milestones, established a configuration-based identity protocol, and enforced a narrative output structure for workflow auditing. Impact: Aligned low-level code execution with advanced research goals, while implementing governance policies to prevent environment drift. tianhe Completed Tasks: Hosted all GPU-accelerated VLA workloads, Pi0 checkpoint integration, E2E promotion tests, and error classifier implementation. Implementation Methods: Managed conda/CUDA runtime, fixed vla_server.py and OpenPI wrappers, performed batch MuJoCo rendering, and resolved external dataset routing issues. Impact: Provided a complete end-to-end error injection capability, fixed critical observation pipeline defects, and established validated baselines for multi-strategy failure analysis. Completed MIHD multimodal fusion research and benchmark tests, conducted key flow matching analysis, implemented error recovery benchmark tests through VLA strategy server integration and natural error capture pipelines, resolved framework API mismatches in Pi0 promotion, and expanded the daily summary CLI infrastructure.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ VLA strategy server integration and E2E promotion execution — Built dedicated TCP inference servers for Pi0/Phoenix models; refactored rollout_generator.py and adapter layer to enable injection/natural capture modes; performed 59+ E2E promotions, capturing 150 baseline failure scenarios. ✅ MIHD fusion research and benchmark optimization — Updated research reports containing flow matching comments, compiled a 21-method fusion table; implemented hidden_dim CLI support to address GCN embedding crashes; conducted parallel benchmark tests on section 151508, proving QFormer Enhanced is superior. ✅ Error recovery benchmark architecture and v4.5 pipeline planning — Reviewed and corrected documentation deviations to align with the real-time registry; designed a dual-track v4.5 roadmap combining natural VLA promotion tests and rule-guided state-aware error detection; implemented Phase 1–6 classification pipelines for three strategy families. ✅ Cross-frame observation mapping and API correction — Resolved OpenPI norm_stats loading mismatches via official API; implemented hierarchical key re-mapping for robustesuite-OpenPI state fusion; eliminated observation/image KeyError, and verified multi-GPU MuJoCo rendering pipelines. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Daily summary CLI and documentation infrastructure extension — Expanded the summary tool to include configuration-based device identity, rclone headless synchronization, and robust ccusage JSON parsing; designed human-readable session-by-session dialogue summaries and result tracking patterns. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. 64-dimensional GCN compression causes severe embedding crashes, with only two active clusters and unreliable visualization output. Solution: Traced the dimensionality bottleneck via variance analysis; quickly deployed configurable hidden_dim ablation experiments in the CLI, planner, and runtime modules to enable systematic diagnostic expansion.
Key Insight: Architecture compression limits quietly trigger representation failures; parameterized ablation capabilities must be implemented before strategic fusion expansion.
2. The standard flow matching architecture is mathematically inappropriate for potential multimodal fusion due to lack of a fixed target distribution. Solution: Concluded that generative mapping lacks necessary supervision signals in the fusion space; shifted to relational methods (AdaLN, contrast learning) and configuration-based integration structures.
Key Insight: Fusion requires relational alignment goals, not generative reconstruction goals; theoretical mismatch dictates early architectural strategy adjustments.
3. Concurrent GPU workloads cause OOM failures and silent caches, masking real-time benchmark progress and resource competition. Solution: Used --override flags to enforce sequential GPU execution, implemented latency space deviation evaluation to suppress memory peaks, and used transparent output streams for reliable monitoring.
Key Insight: In shared HPC environments, resource isolation and explicit state coverage mechanisms are essential; silent background failures reduce verification integrity and require active management.
4. VLA server initialization fails due to OpenPI API mismatches and flat/hierarchical key conflicts, preventing image pipelines from reaching the strategy model. Solution: Replaced custom norm_stats processing with create_trained_policy; injected a clear IMAGE_KEY_MAP re-mapping into the strategy adapter to align robosuite output with LiberoInputs mode.
Key Insight: Cross simulator integration requires strict adherence to internal configuration dictionaries; reliance on generic wrappers leads to versioning and format fragility.
General Issues 5. Documentation drift and parallel YAML editing introduce structural duplicates and incorrect registry counts, threatening downstream context accuracy. Solution: Performed real-time comparison checks and enumeration of the code library; applied automatic pattern validation to eliminate isolated configuration blocks, ensuring single-source truth.
Key Insight: Unverified documentation triggers severe hallucination; all architecture or milestone updates must be anchored with an automatic registry.
Human and AI Approaches Strategic Level Fusion Methodology and Target Distribution Constraints | Role | Method | |——|——| | Human | Identified theoretical contradictions between FM requirements and fusion tasks, defined a dual-axis evaluation matrix, and required relational approaches instead of generative methods. | | AI | Initially treated updates as sequential editing/code execution; later assisted by constructing theoretical counterexamples and validating architectural adjustments. |
Analysis of Differences: Humans provide domain-aware feasibility evaluations and practical ranking frameworks; AI acts as an efficient document executor and structure synthesizer.
VLA Integration Strategy and System Boundaries Role Method Human Defined strategic architecture boundaries, prioritized natural errors over manual injections, and emphasized stability of pre-trained encoders rather than expensive fine-tuning. AI Generated detailed interface architecture diagrams, tracked external library APIs item by item, and handled tactical payload mapping and state extractor alignment issues. Analysis of Differences: Humans focus on high-level environment isolation, measurement validity, and production readiness; AI compensates for implementation flaws through low-level dependency checks.
Documentation Verification Paradigm Role Method Human Required validation based on real data registry and enumeration before approving changes, rather than relying on document strings or Markdown summaries. AI Initially relied on numbers in documents and standard grep patterns, verifying through prior context rather than real-time code state. Analysis of Differences: Humans use audit and verification thinking to ensure structural authenticity; AI initially relied on surface-level pattern matching until forced to obtain independent real data.
Implementation Level Architecture Modularity and Configuration Switching Role Method Human Prioritized configuration-based enhancements to prevent pipeline fragmentation and reduce integration overhead. AI Proposed creating independent strategy branches for each method to maintain standard software engineering modularity. Analysis of Differences: Humans strategically choose simple configuration switching to avoid system chaos; AI initially favors maximum modularity, despite increasing integration complexity.
AI Limitations Key Limitations Initially propagated incorrect configuration counts, assuming local checkpoints were available, relying on prior context or cache data, until forced to validate via real-time code library and shared storage. Encapsulated abstract boundaries (such as internal state extractor wrappers) delayed root cause diagnosis during deep integration; architecture tracing prompts are needed to bypass surface-level debugging. General Limitations Failed to anticipate CLI flags for incompatible target environments, and handled畸形 JSON Schema from external diagnostic tools without explicit type checking. Difficult to manage long-running background GPU processes and dynamic resource allocation; requires manual process termination and explicit flag覆盖, rather than reliable asynchronous task retrieval. Lessons Learned Key Experiences Extreme dimensionality compression in graph-based fusion triggers silent representation crashes; statistical variance checks must be performed before visual clustering evaluation to prevent computational waste. Cross-frame observation mapping is the most fragile integration layer; clear hierarchical key re-mapping and official model loading API prevent version mismatches and pipeline interruptions. Documentation drift directly destroys downstream AI context windows; treating Markdown artifacts as live code with registry validation prevents cascading hallucinations. Claude Code CLI effectively serves as a local multimodal VLM backend; script-based calls enable frame-level visual debugging, superior to generic remote API endpoints. Practical Experience Head-to-desktop synchronization and cross-storage verification require explicit identity markers, dynamic resource checks, and robust fallback parsers to handle unpredictable external tool outputs. Impact: Transformed the tool architecture into a highly resilient structure, eliminated JSON corruption risks and duplicate API token consumption issues, significantly reduced module maintenance overhead, and prevented configuration drift. tianhe Completed work: Executed Error Recovery Benchmark v4.2 planning, fixed critical errors in MuJoCo visualization caused by high Kp controller injected force, expanded scenario generation to 118 samples, and designed a two-layer VLM/rule-based error classification framework. Implementation methods: During injection windows, converted post-error deployment actions into neutral vectors to bypass trajectory tracking compensation mechanisms; extended RolloutGenerator and introduced pluggable PolicyAdapter interfaces for base models; applied force reapplication logic for each step; integrated the academic fault classification system into a structured nested implementation roadmap. Impact: Eliminated critical tracking errors, restored observable motion in videos, and established an extensible infrastructure independent of policies suitable for autonomous AI error evaluation, without blocking current research development cycles. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Deployed Hugo static site and archived historical daily reports — Converted Markdown reference blocks into standard YAML preamble information, executed update.sh build pipeline to generate 139 pages of content covering bugJournal entries, verified dual-repo git status, and pushed production resources to GitHub Pages. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. MuJoCo’s high-gain OSC controllers compensate for injected force by using demonstration actions to cover trajectories, resulting in complete lack of motion errors in visual videos despite normal backend logs. Solution: Divide post-error deployment into three independent stages: neutral force application, weak stability window using specialized parameters, and demonstration recovery. During injection, explicitly switch the action source to neutral vectors to disable motion tracking feedback loops.
Key insight: Robot controllers with high gain ratios immediately cancel external forces during active tracking; to completely eliminate error performance, control loops must be isolated through non-tracking phases.
2. Sudden interruptions or Ctrl+C crashes during Gadget CLI file writing cause partial JSON files, leading to downstream parsing failures and damaged daily report status. Solution: Implemented _atomic_write, used tempfile.mkstemp to safely process before output draft, and then immediately renamed it via os.replace. A defensive fallback mechanism allows graceful handling of partial writes without leaving corrupted data on disk.
Key insight: Atomic file system operations are the industry standard for崩溃 resilience in Python pipelines; tempfiles + renaming are more reliable than complex locking mechanisms to prevent partial state damage.
3. The automatic benchmark scheduler cannot properly allocate heterogeneous workloads, causing heavy neural components (such as Q-Former) to fail due to CUDA OOM, leading to neglect of lightweight baseline evaluations and parallel scGPT runtime crashes. Solution: Dynamically reconfigured the pipeline, split heavy Q-Former batches, and forced epoch reduction to 50 to accelerate iteration without sacrificing quality consistency. Rearranged experiment queues based on resource profiles rather than static order, and enforced memory partitioning.
Key insight: Dynamic scheduling is significantly better than static order execution in multi-device environments; decoupling pipeline evaluation stages prevents severe resource starvation and reduces total benchmark completion time on limited HPC nodes.
4. The Gadget export pipeline re-summarized merged operations, causing AI API duplicate consumption, token waste, and unnecessary latency. Solution: Inserted _merged_devices tracking arrays into the local export JSON. The merged/export process now checks these local source markers before any cloud LLM call, ensuring strict idempotence of multi-device aggregation.
Key insight: Local state protection at data input points is an important cost optimization strategy for distributed pipelines and prevents duplicate cloud interactions.
5. Google Calendar timezone detection causes frequent noisy 403禁止 warnings due to insufficient OAuth scope provided by calendarList().get() API endpoints. Solution: Immediately conduct OAuth scope audits and redirect API requests to calendar.events permissions consistent with the granted settings().get(), and implement direct configuration fallback mechanisms to eliminate duplicate failure logs.
Key insight: OAuth scope audits must be performed before feature implementation; relying on assumed broad permissions leads to silent failures, excessive noise logs, and expensive manual fallback chains, requiring targeted API adjustments.
General Issues 6. Benchmark scenario generation initially produced only tip_over errors because the ProximityDetector consumed all demonstration quotas, leaving the friction and pose_perturb injectors without generation capability. Solution: Re-designed targeted modifications, diversified detector specifications in configuration files, increased max_scenes_per_demo allocation budget, and established clear detector-level type routing logic.
Key insight: Unchecked quota competition among automatic detection systems concentrates output in the most frequently triggered categories; clear budget allocation or priority weighted routing is needed to maintain diversity in benchmark tests.

Difference analysis: Humans focus on strategic cost optimization, module decoupling, and resilient export priorities; AI quickly implemented the structure, but defaults to compatibility with older versions rather than seeking cross-device optimization.

Difference Analysis: The human successfully guides strategic shift and hypothesis generation, while the AI performs a rigorous technical gap analysis, extracts transferable structural concepts, and correctly identifies constraints that do not apply to the robot domain, such as FAST tokenization.
AI Limitations Key Limitations When the interactive planning tool (e.g., ExitPlanMode) is interrupted by the user, the execution context is lost and state boundaries cannot be preserved, forcing reliance on explicit manual planning injections to restore accurate implementation without guessing. The initial default reactive approach to problem-solving (later fixes) instead of designing preventive state protection mechanisms during the initial data export or pipeline design phase indicates a gap in active infrastructure optimization reasoning. General Limitations Lack of active cross-site awareness: Initially, the double-repo architecture standard in Hugo deployment (separation of source code and static website artefacts) was not anticipated, requiring explicit human intervention to prevent version control conflicts. Tendency to verify visual or structural success through exit codes and raw logs rather than directly confirming state, leading to premature termination of physical debugging tasks that require kinematic verification. The export pipeline must retain clear local device state markers (e.g., _source_device or _merged_devices) to enable safe and repeatable multi-device aggregation, avoiding race conditions or severe cloud API token costs. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. MIHD Benchmark: Redundant embedding computation — The same gene/visual encoder was run hundreds of times for different fusion strategies (for example, PCA was calculated 55 times, UNI2 was calculated 77 times) Solution: A two-stage pipeline was designed: in the first stage, all encoder embeddings were extracted and cached (duplication reduction, 110 tasks corresponding to 286 experiments = 62% reduction); in the second stage, the cached embeddings were loaded and only fusion+clustering+evaluation were performed. Now the UNI2 model is loaded only once across all 11 parts, instead of 77 times. Key insight: The current cache uses {gene}_{vision}_{fusion}/{section}_embeddings.npz as a key containing the fusion name, so changing the fusion method causes re-extraction. Encoder-level caching gene_cache/{encoder}/{section}.npz, vision_cache/{encoder}/{section}.npz enables significant reuse. Reuse of model instances across different parts also provides additional performance gains.
2. Error recovery benchmark: Force applied to the wrong body part (using bin2 instead of gripper EEF), no abnormal behavior observed in video Solution: Detailed logs revealed that force was applied to bin2. Root cause: _get_eef_body_name() lacked “gripper0_eef” in the possible name list, and the geometric fallback search matched robot0_screen_collision (containing “ee”) → bin2. The problem was solved by adding “gripper0_eef”, “robot0_right_hand”, and “gripper0_gripper_base” to the possible name list.
Key insight: The EEF body names for different robots are different (Sawyer uses gripper0_eef, not the generic gripper_link), which must be explicitly included in the possible name list. Falling back to geometric search may cause strings containing “ee” to match irrelevant geometric models.
3. Error recovery benchmark: PreGrasp detector never triggers — get_task_phase() always returns “unknown” Solution: Root cause: get_task_phase() called _check_phase_condition(), which is an empty implementation that always returns False. All dependent on task_phase detectors (PreGrasp, GraspPrecond) are affected. The complete phase detection logic is in get_task_completion_stages(). The problem was solved by rewriting get_task_phase() to use sensor-based detection. Multiple cascading errors were also fixed: forward view used a neutral action instead of a demonstration action, the proximity door prevented pre-contact detector activation, global cooling time made simultaneous detection impossible, and MuJoCo body names did not match.
Key insight: There is a working implementation get_task_completion_stages in the code library and an always-failing empty implementation _check_phase_condition; callers used the wrong method. The symptom is the detector not triggering, but the root cause is dead code in the infrastructure layer. When logical contradictions are observed (no rejection but no output), infrastructure auditing should be prioritized over symptom debugging.
4. Error recovery benchmark: duration_steps configuration parameter invalid — all forces lasted only 1 step (0.05 seconds) Solution: MuJoCo automatically clears xfrc_applied after each sim.step. Solution: Modify collect_rollout_stats() to call injector.apply() repeatedly during the first duration_steps of the validation process, and call injector.clear() after the duration ends.
Key insight: MuJoCo’s xfrc_applied is a persistent field but is automatically cleared; the application layer needs to re-applicate each step explicitly to maintain force application. This is a system-level error affecting all error types.
5. Error recovery benchmark: 30N force not observed in visualization video of robot arm movement Solution: Add --force_override parameter to test larger forces without regeneration; update the force range in configuration to 15–45N. The problem persists at 30N — further investigation is needed into the force mechanism (possibly too strong OSC control loop, too short force duration at 1 step, or incorrect xfrc_applied application).
Key insight: The force injection mechanism works properly (xfrc_applied is set/clear), but 30N may not be sufficient against the 150 N/m stiffness of the OSC controller, or the duration at 1 step (about 20 ms) is too short for visible effects. The OSC control loop may suppress external forces within one control cycle.
6. CalendarPro: Users cannot delete multiple calendar events that match a pattern (e.g., “Cancel all GB teacher meetings before March 1”) — the robot only says “Please specify the events to delete” Solution: The data model was extended to support date ranges and batch operations, the LLM prompt was updated to extract these fields, the search function was modified to accept custom time windows, and an interactive confirmation interface with Discord buttons was added, showing a preview and clear approval options.
Key insight: For productivity tools, single CRUD operations are insufficient — batch operations with safety confirmation (preview + user explicit approval) are crucial for user workflows involving patterns.
7. Gadget/summarize: Headless server cannot install cloud storage application to achieve automatic synchronization Solution: Researched and integrated the rclone CLI tool, supporting token-based replication authentication (run rclone authorize on a machine using a browser, copy the token to the headless server).
Key insight: rclone supports over 70 cloud providers; token-based replication headless authentication is the best cross-platform cloud CLI option.
8. Error recovery benchmark: Global cooling time prevents pre-grasp detector activation when proximity detection triggers first Solution: Implement tracking of each detector’s cooling time (cooldown_counters dictionary) so each detector has independent cooling time. Filter detection results to exclude detectors still in cooling state.
Key insight: Global cooling time is unsuitable for multiple detector systems because different detectors target different stages/conditions. A multi-detector system requires cooling time tracking for each detector.
9. CalendarPro: When a user message occurs, Google Calendar API returns 403 insufficientPermissions, causing a console warning Solution: Switch from calendarList().get() API to settings().get(setting=‘timezone’) API, which only requires the calendar.events scope instead of broader calendar access permissions.
Key insight: Different Google Calendar API endpoints require different OAuth scopes — for timezone retrieval, the settings API has lower permission requirements than calendarList API.
10. CalendarPro: When the LLM times out (nested Claude Code environment), batch deletion fails because intent.data is empty — semantic router correctly classified the intent but did not extract structured data Solution: Add a raw_input penetration mechanism in the handler, implement_extract_delete_query() and use regular expression patterns to parse search keywords from Chinese/English phrases, and add date extraction patterns to identify ranges like “before March 1”.
Key insight: The double verification system needs independent extraction capabilities in both paths — relying solely on SR fallback or LLM-generated structured data is insufficient.
11. Gadget/summarize: ccusage –offline mode shows Opus 4.6 price as $0 Solution: Remove –offline parameter and switch to online mode to get the latest model price.
Key insight: The offline pricing table does not include the latest model (e.g., Opus 4.6); online access is needed for accurate billing information. Although online mode is slightly slower, data accuracy is more important.
12. Error recovery benchmark: Proximity door (max_eef_object_distance=0.05m) prevents Pregrasp operations within 0.05–0.1m Solution: Add detector names to bypass the door detection list — detectors with self-distance validation (pregrasp, grasp_precond) skip door detection.
Key insight: The proximity door is designed for contact-based detectors but is incorrectly applied to all detectors regardless of operating distance. Constraints of specific detectors should not be covered by global door detection.
13. CalendarPro & gadget/summarize: Nested Claude code session blocks and Claude CLI subprocess calls cause always-timeout classification by large language model during developmentSolution: CalendarPro tried to cancel CLAUDECODE environment variables when starting subprocesses but still failed — the final solution is to test in an external independent environment. Gadget/summarize successfully canceled CLAUDECODE and CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRY in the subprocess environment. Key insight: Development environment tools may interfere with the tested system in non-intuitive ways — AI service calls via subprocess are particularly sensitive to environmental interference. Subprocesses inherit parent environment variables and need explicit removal.
14. Gadget/summarize: Windows subprocess cannot find npx (.cmd file) Solution: Add shell=True parameter to the subprocess.run call.
Key insight: Windows npm global commands are actually .cmd files, and Python subprocesses do not parse them by default; shell execution is required.

Key insight: LLM output format is unstable; multiple fallback mechanisms are needed to ensure stability.

General Issues 17. CalendarPro: BatchDeleteApprovalView returns an empty string after sending a confirmation via channel.send(), causing the main loop to fail when trying to send an empty message to the Discord API Solution: Add an ‘if response:’ check before message.channel.send(response) to skip sending when the response is empty.

Lessons Learned Key Experience – Two-Stage Pipeline Mode in the Experiment Matrix: When running M encoder × N fusion × K parts, divide it into stage 1 (M × K encoding tasks with cache) and stage 2 (M × N × K evaluation tasks loaded from cache). Reducing redundant computation O(M × N × K) to O(M × K + M × N × K) through shared encoding. Cache key design is important: encoder-level cache allows sharing between different fusion steps.- MuJoCo xfrc_applied behavior: Although the documentation indicates that xfrc_applied is retained between calls, mj_step() automatically clears it. To achieve persistence, the application layer must explicitly reapply each step. It must be explicitly cleared via injector.clear() after duration_steps to achieve a true pulse behavior. STUB methods and complete implementations coexist with code smells: When a function contains a complete logic but the caller always uses a stub that fails, the call relationships should be reviewed immediately rather than debugging parameters. When logical contradictions (no rejection but no output) are observed, infrastructure auditing should be prioritized over symptom debugging. Force injection visualization balance: An OSC controller with KP=150 N/m requires at least ≥25N of force to see displacement, but the OSC control loop may suppress external forces during a control cycle (about 20ms). A careful balance between force magnitude and duration is needed. Productivity tools need batch operations with security mechanisms: (1) pattern matching to find multiple items, (2) preview of affected items, (3) explicit user confirmation before execution. Single-item CRUD operations are insufficient for actual workflows. rclone is the best cross-platform cloud CLI choice, supporting over 70 providers, and enables headless authentication via token replication (run rclone authorize on a machine in the browser, then copy the token to the headless server). Model reuse between batches: For a visual encoder that processes multiple parts, the model only needs to be loaded once for reuse between parts, without reloading each part. The initialization cost of the model is reduced from O(number_of_parts) to O(1). This is crucial for large Transformers like UNI2. Risk of mismatch in fallback mechanisms: When the main method fails, falling back to a stricter match (such as geometric name search) may produce incorrect results (“ee” matching the screen rather than the end effector). The fallback path requires additional verification. EEF body names vary between robots (Sawyer uses gripper0_eef instead of the general gripper_link), which needs to be explicitly included. Simplified detection logic for step-changing systems: For discrete state systems (such as the step change of the gripper 0→1), detection based on continuity (decreased distance, proximity) is unreliable; the state change itself should be checked directly (whether it is different after N steps). Multi-detector systems require tracking of each detector’s cooling time — global cooling may incorrectly prevent simultaneous detection from different sources. Detector-specific constraints (distance thresholds, phase requirements) should not be covered by global gates — let the detector verify itself. The OAuth permission requirements between Google Calendar API endpoints vary greatly — setting up the API requires lower permissions for the same information (timezone) than the calendarList API. A dual-validation system (semantic router + LLM) needs independent extraction capabilities in both paths — it cannot be assumed that the LLM always generates structured output. The pricing table for ccusage offline mode does not include the latest models (such as Opus 4.6); it needs to be obtained online for accurate billing. Although the online mode is slightly slower, data accuracy is more important. Windows child process calls to .cmd files require shell=True; otherwise, the globally installed npm command cannot be found. Visual encoding bottlenecks: (1) the serial patch extraction loop is limited by CPU (3000–4000 iterations). (2) Calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() approximately 100 times after each batch brings significant overhead. (3) The hard-coded batch_size=32 may not be ideal. Performance analysis is needed before optimization. Environment switching based on child processes: When dependencies require different conda environments, use child processes to call scripts in the target environment instead of trying to switch inside Python. User feedback should be detailed and specific — for calendar operations, always include: what operation was performed, which events were affected, and the time of occurrence. The development environment may interfere with the testing system — nested Claude Code sessions block AI service calls based on child processes. Child processes inherit parent environment variables, and specific variables (such as CLAUDECODE) need to be explicitly removed to avoid nested detection. JSON parsing requires multi-level fallback to handle various formats of LLM output: direct parsing → extracting code blocks → searching for {to} substrings. The LLM output format is unstable, so robustness is required. The priority order of configuration files should be: CLI parameters > environment variables > configuration files > default values, to ensure flexibility and overrideability. The choice of deduplication key should be based on the minimum field combination that uniquely identifies entities. For dialogue: (source, project, timestamp). Practical Experience When the processor directly sends messages via channels (for interactive UI), it should return an empty string indicating “processed”. The main loop must check ‘if response:’ before sending. Testing showed no robot interference. Through detailed debug logs, it was found that force was applied to bin2 instead of the gripper EEF. The root cause: _get_eef_body_name() lacked “gripper0_eef”. After fixing, videos for 30N and infinite force were generated for verification.

error_recovery_benchmark ✅ Fix of PreGrasp detector not triggering problem + dead code cleanup 22:56:34.002 | claude_code Two-part plan was implemented: (1) rewrite get_task_phase() to use get_task_completion_stages() instead of the stub, thereby enabling phase detection. (2) remove dead rejection tracking code.
