content:
Daily Report — 2026-02-13 General Overview Completed Tasks: Four major projects are progressing well: MIHD benchmark data repair and architecture planning, toolkit refactoring and open-sourcing, robot error recovery framework completion, and CalendarPro production environment optimization with intelligent features. Implementation Methods: Through systematic root cause analysis, modular architecture design, two-stage pipeline mode, comprehensive testing coverage (over 107 tests per project), reasonable asynchronous lifecycle management, and dual-language documentation writing. Impact: MIHD is ready for use in 286 experiments with complete spatial data; the toolkit supports cross-device collaboration workflows and is open-sourced; the error recovery infrastructure is completed with a full demonstration replay function; CalendarPro is ready with automatic learning, personalized energy prediction, and thought organization features. DCC Completed Tasks: MIHD spatial transcriptome benchmark: data repair (4 failed parts) and complete 7-stage optimization plan design (standardization/Q-Former/LLaVA MLP/Niche/BatchCorrection/multi-stage configuration refactoring). Implementation Methods: Extracting missing spatial coordinates from Dataset.zip, fixing frequency filter boundary checks, adding mclust→KMeans fallback mechanism, repairing GPU monitoring threads; analyzing the code library (config_manager.py 590 lines, run_benchmark.py 2600 lines) and QueST reference implementation, writing independent plans with exact line numbers. Impact: All 11 DLPFC parts now operate normally with complete spatial data; comprehensive phases 1 to 7 blueprints provide detailed implementation roadmaps including precise integration points and dependencies. MacBook Completed Tasks: Toolkit optimization: refactoring the daily summary tool into a two-stage multi-device architecture (export→merge), integrating ccusage token statistics, initializing a Git repository with complete documentation. Implementation Methods: Redesigning daily_summary.py via CLI subcommands, adding device information collection functionality, designing recoverable JSON log format, using subprocess for token statistics; creating .gitignore file, managing test/ as a git submodule, writing 7 README files covering all tools. Impact: The daily report tool now supports cross-device collaboration workflows and automatically tracks token usage; the toolkit repository is open-sourced on GitHub with complete documentation, improving maintainability. tianhe Completed Tasks: Error recovery benchmark: completed v4.1 infrastructure (4/4 validators, video annotations), diagnosed and fixed critical demonstration replay environment mismatches through three-layer root cause analysis, reducing documentation from 615 lines to 101 lines. Implementation Methods: Implementing LargeOffsetValidator and StuckValidator, achieving 41 tests passed; adding frame annotations based on cv2; identifying mismatches between PickPlace_D0+ controller configuration and basic PickPlace configuration by loading env_args from HDF5 metadata; systematic code cleanup, removing approximately 190 dead lines. Impact: Scene generation efficiency increased 10 times (3 scenes → 30 scenes), EEF distance control is more precise (5cm vs 22cm); trigger steps execute during demonstration when the robot approaches objects; documentation size reduced to 1/6 of the original, making it more practical and concise. TzJsDesktop Completed Tasks: Major CalendarPro version release: implementing automatic scheduling system for periodic tasks, fixing production environment vulnerabilities (double verification mismatch, error merging, duplicate event modification), completing P0 reliability fixes and P1 intelligent upgrades, building automatic organization function for random ideas, comprehensive documentation update. Implementation Methods: Creating RecurringTaskStore with JSONL persistence and PeriodicChecker with asyncio background loop; fixing dual_verify.py, prioritizing LLM over semantic router; adding CalendarServiceError exception propagation mechanism; implementing JSON parsing resilience, 30-second timeout for AI provider, message queue completion callback; adding automatic learning data collection and personalized energy prediction; building a thought capture system with idle detection and AI organization. Impact: 107/110 tests passed; users now see detailed error messages instead of silent failures; the system automatically learns from user behavior for personalized energy prediction; automatic scheduling of periodic tasks; capturing short thoughts during idle time and organizing them into target levels. A full day of multi-project development: repairing MIHD spatial transcriptome data issues and designing 7-stage optimization plans; refactoring the toolkit daily report tool into a two-stage multi-device architecture and establishing a Git repository; implementing error recovery benchmark validators and fixing critical demonstration replay environment mismatches; building CalendarPro automatic scheduling, fixing production vulnerabilities, and implementing P0/P1 roadmaps and random idea functions.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy - ✅ Design MIHD 7-stage enhancement plan — Studied the code library and QueST reference documents, designed phases 1 to 7: configuration refactoring, standardized integration, UNI2+scGPT experiments, Q-Former/LLaVA MLP fusion, specific queries, batch correction, multi-stage modes. Completed complete independent plans with specific line numbers, stored in mutable-riding-eclipse.md ✅ Fix demonstration replay environment configuration mismatch — Applied three-layer root cause analysis, identified differences between PickPlace_D0+ controller configuration and pure PickPlace configuration; loading env_args from HDF5 metadata; fixing the proximity threshold after recovery. ✅ Fix CalendarPro double verification intent mismatch — Modified dual_verify.py, prioritizing LLM intent over semantic router when conflicts occur because LLM has a complete dialogue context, while SR only matches keywords. ✅ Add CalendarPro calendar error reporting function — Refactored calendar_service.py to throw CalendarServiceError instead of silent failure; updated all processors (discord_bot, scheduler, api_routes) to capture and display detailed error messages. ✅ Fix MIHD 4 failed chapter data issues — Extracting missing spatial files from Dataset.zip (tissue_positions_list.csv, scalefactors_json.json, images); fixing frequency filtering boundary checks; adding mclust→KMeans fallback mechanism. ✅ Refactor gadget daily summary into two-stage architecture — Redesigning daily_summary.py, adding CLI subcommands (export/merge/legacy); adding device information collection functionality; designing versioned JSON log format; implementing token usage statistics. ✅ Implement CalendarPro periodic task system — Creating RecurringTaskStore with JSONL persistence and PeriodicChecker using asyncio background loop (15-minute interval), adding MANAGE_RECURRING/QUERY_RECURRING intentions, semantic routing, Discord integration. All 18 tests passed. ✅ Fix CalendarPro periodic event modification issues — Modifying the update_event() function, detecting periodic instances before updating and removing recurrence/recurringEventId fields, so Google Calendar only produces anomalies for a single instance. ✅ Create CalendarPro PLANNING.md document — Writing a comprehensive planning document with over 330 lines, covering project positioning, module maturity ratings, target levels, architecture decisions and reasons, P0-P3 roadmaps, known defects. ✅ CalendarPro P0 reliability fix — Implementing three-stage fallback JSON parsing resilience, setting 30-second timeout for AI provider (asyncio.wait_for + httpx.Timeout), message queue completion callback, service layer error handling, performing 56 intent classification boundary tests. ✅ CalendarPro P1 intelligent upgrade — Implementing automatic learning data collection via backfill_energy_change(), personalized energy prediction through personalize_rhythm(), integrating learning functions into IntelligentScheduler, improving dialogue context format. ✅ Implement CalendarPro random thinking function — Building a complete thought set system: using ThoughtStore stored in JSONL,复用 EssentialScheduler’s IdleDetector, with ThoughtOrganizer with background asyncio loop, integrated with Discord via 3 processor methods, all 25 tests passed. ✅ Write gadget comprehensive documentation — Writing independent READMEs (summarize/Video/audio/image/papers/git/test) for 7 tools, creating a root README with tool overview table, and a quick start guide summarize/tutorial.md. ✅ Fix MuJoCo speed exchange error — Fixing env_wrapper.py, treating cvel[3:] as linear speed, cvel[:3] as angular speed (MuJoCo stores [angular speed, linear speed]). ✅ Implement error recovery validators (LargeOffset, Stuck) — Creating large_offset.py and stuck.py validators, including configuration sections and 16 unit tests (8 each), completing 4/4 validator suite. ✅ Compress error recovery CLAUDE.md document — Reducing line count from 615 to 101 by eliminating duplicate content, removing inappropriate README content, merging chapters, focusing on non-obvious information. ✅ Enhance visualization with frame annotations — Adding annotations based on cv2: stage color banner (green/red/orange), semi-transparent information boxes showing detection/injection/verification details, frame count. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Initialize gadget Git repository — Creating .gitignore, git init, pointing test/ as a submodule to TzJ2006/test.git, committing and pushing to git@github.com:TzJ2006/gadget.git. ✅ Integrate ccusage token statistics — Calling npx ccusage via subprocess to add fetch_ccusage() function, parsing JSON output; integrating into three entry points; displaying token usage section in markdown reports. ✅ Update CalendarPro documentation — Adding 10 previously unrecorded systems to CLAUDE.md; expanding README with 4 types of usage examples, Discord command references, learning system documentation; adding PowerShell startup script. 🔄 Error recovery code cleanup — Phase 1 completed: removing approximately 190 dead lines (ReplaySystem, ReplayDriftError, duplicate detect() method); commenting BCPolicy stub. Phases 2 to 5 interrupted. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. The error recovery robot never approaches objects during demonstration replay (minimum distance 0.22 meters, task requires contact) Solution: By tracking robosuite source code, HDF5 metadata, and MuJoCo body mapping, it was found that the demonstration recorded with PickPlace_D0+ controller configuration is replayed in pure PickPlace mode. The same operation produces a completely different trajectory.
Key Insight: Environmental configuration (including kp, damping, slope ratio controller configurations) fundamentally changes robot dynamics. Always using accurate environmental metadata from HDF5 dataset for replay — parameter adjustments cannot cover the fundamental issue.
2. CalendarPro semantic router and LLM conflict, causing incorrect routing by default (e.g., ‘leetcode’ keyword → manage_recurring instead of update)Solution: dual_verify.py was modified to prioritize LLM intent over SR when conflicts occur. LLMs possess a complete conversation context, whereas SR only matches keywords. The log message ‘→ using LLM intent’ is used for monitoring. Key Insight: Classifiers based on keywords fail with ambiguous expressions. When semantic routers and LLMs disagree, the model with more context (LLM) should be trusted instead of faster SR. SR filters obvious cases, and LLMs act as arbitrators.
3. Missing data in MIHD Chapter 4 leads to process failure (space files, empty regions in frequency filtering, STAIG model crash) Solution: Extract space files from Dataset.zip; add boundary checks (min_w/min_h >= 10); add mclust to the fallback mechanism of KMeans, using a try/except wrapper.
Key Insight: Spatial transcriptomic data requires strong fault tolerance: multi-path candidate search, image processing boundary checks, and statistical model fallback strategies to handle distribution anomalies.
4. The original single-step workflow of gadget cannot support multi-device collaboration (log must be manually copied to each device) Solution: Reconstructed into a two-stage process: (1) A sub-command is used to create local JSON logs, which include device information without an API key; (2) The sub-commands are merged to aggregate multiple logs and call the API to generate the final report; the old mode is retained to ensure backward compatibility. Key Insight: Multi-device workflows require a portable intermediate format (versioned JSON logs) and clear stage separation (local parsing and remote merging). Key design elements: device information collection, version features supporting future expansion, optional device-level summaries to prevent information loss during merging.
5. All error detectors fail after adding the neighboring threshold—after adjusting the iteration threshold (0.05→0.15→0.25→0.30m), no triggering event occurs. Solution: A diagnostic script was written to measure the actual EEF-object distance, revealing that the issue is environmental mismatch rather than a threshold problem. The root cause is the replay configuration, not the sensitivity of the detector.
Key Insight: When all detectors fail, the true value should be measured via diagnostic logs, and then the threshold should be adjusted. Symptoms of no triggering events often hide the underlying mismatch (controller dynamic errors).
6. CalendarPro calendar API errors (403 insufficientPermissions, HttpError) are output via print() and return None, causing users to be troubled by a generic “failure” message. Solution: A CalendarServiceError exception is created; all calendar_service methods are refactored to throw exceptions with detailed context; all callers are updated to capture and display user-friendly messages containing technical details.
Key Insight: Silent error handling (print + returning None) breaks the error contract. Users cannot fix issues they cannot see. Errors with context should always be passed to the presentation layer, followed by appropriate formatting.
7. CalendarPro AI provider lacks a timeout mechanism—network latency may cause the entire robot to halt indefinitely. Solution: All API calls are wrapped with asyncio.wait_for(timeout=30.0), and httpx.Timeout(30.0) is added in the client constructor. When the timeout occurs, an AIResponse containing error fields is returned.
Key Insight: Timeout protection requires dual layers: asyncio coroutine level (wait_for) and HTTP client level (httpx.Timeout) to capture different failure modes.
8. CalendarPro JSON parsing failure occurs when the AI returns text, multiple blocks, or truncated JSON before JSON—leading to intent classification failure. Solution: The _extract_json() method is implemented to extract the first complete object by balancing the bracket count; a three-stage fallback (direct parsing → trailing comma repair → general intent) is added; ValueError exceptions are removed for logging and fallback use.
Key Insight: Production-level AI systems need graceful degradation—never crash on malformed output, always provide a safe fallback intent.
9. The planning document lacks self-containedness—users repeatedly reject the ExitPlanMode mode, demanding “writing every word of the plan into the plan file”. Solution: The planning document is rewritten to be fully self-contained: user decision records are added, code snapshots with exact line numbers are included, QueST reference code details are provided, complete implementation code with “inserted after line X” locations are included, and corresponding positions for each stage are given.
Key Insight: Planning mode documents must be fully self-contained for future session recovery. User rejection signals indicate insufficient details—all exploration results (exact positions, line numbers, function signatures, existing code) must be written into the plan; external context cannot be relied upon.
10. MuJoCo speed swap causes false instability triggers (angular velocity is misread as linear). Solution: Array slices are swapped: linvel = cvel[3:], angvel = cvel[:3] to match MuJoCo’s [angular(3), linear(3)] layout.
Key Insight: Documentation mismatch: code comments claim [linear, angular], but MuJoCo stores [angular, linear]. Always verify against the source document, not inline comments.
11. Error recovery CLAUDE.md has 615 lines, with many repetitions between sections, and some content belongs to the README file. Solution: The document is rewritten, focusing on: (1) Information that is difficult to discover (server limits, common pitfalls); (2) Merging commands into a single block; (3) Removing easily discoverable content (file tree, method signatures); (4) Keeping only architectures that require multi-file reading.
Key Insight: AI agent documentation should focus on content that cannot be discovered via tools, rather than a comprehensive reference. Simplicity improves usability—101 lines vs. 615 lines, and it is clearer.
12. When CalendarPro updates repeated events, it modifies the entire series instead of a single instance, even though singleEvents=True is used during search. Solution: The update_event() method is modified to detect repeated instances (has recurringEventId), and the duplicate/recurringEventId fields are removed before calling the API. Google Calendar only generates an exception for that instance.
Key Insight: Implicit behavior of Google Calendar API: singleEvents=True during search provides instance IDs, but update/delete requires explicit removal of fields to avoid series-wide changes. Always test repeated operations on a test calendar.
13. CalendarPro asyncio.create_task() used for the message queue has no exception callback—tasks may silently die in the full queue, and user messages are never processed. Solution: done_callback=_on_queue_task_done is added to all create_task calls; a cleanup processor is implemented to record exceptions and remove dead tasks; a close() method is added for closing.
Key Insight: Asyncio background tasks are defaultly “forgotten”—always add done callbacks for monitoring/cleanup, especially long-running tasks.
General Issues 14. Manually checking token usage is cumbersome—users want automated daily statistics. Solution: ccusage@latest daily –json is called via subprocess to integrate with ccusage, output is parsed; collected automatically at three entry points; a token usage section is rendered with a total table and model details; data is merged across devices for aggregation.
Key Insight: Use existing tools for automated data collection instead of reimplementing them. Design considerations: fault tolerance of subprocess (silently skip if unavailable), multi-device aggregation strategy (summarize tokens/costs, merge model details), readable presentation format (tables are better than lists).
15. MIHD GPU peak statistics always remain zero (ResourceMonitor never calls update_peak_stats()). Solution: ResourceMonitor is refactored: start_monitoring() starts a daemon thread for sampling per second, stop_monitoring() terminates the thread and samples the final peak, threading.Event is used for lifecycle control.
Key Insight: Monitoring peak statistics requires continuous sampling during operation, not just start/stop snapshots. Background daemon threads are a standard solution, but proper lifecycle management is needed to avoid resource leakage.
16. The gadget test/ directory is a nested git repository containing its own remote repository, causing conflicts with git add on nested repositories. Solution: git submodule is used: test files are moved to a backup, ‘git submodule add git@github.com:TzJ2006/test.git test’ is used to clone to the correct commit, the backup is removed, and .gitmodules automatically records the configuration.
Summary All issues were resolved through tool integration, code refactoring, and architecture optimization, maintaining the original Markdown format. Key Insight: Git submodules are suitable for nested repositories with independent remote repositories. Key points: submodules record commit hashes rather than branches; ‘git submodule update –init –recursive’ is required during cloning; updates require entering the submodule directory, executing git pull, and then committing to change the hash.
17. CalendarPro start.bat cannot detect the conda environment (CONDA_PREFIX is unavailable in a new cmd window, cmd does not support ‘conda activate’ without conda init). Solution: A start.ps1 file containing native PowerShell conda support is created; ‘conda activate calendarpro’ can be executed directly in PowerShell. start.bat is updated to use -Powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to delegate execution; PID tracking and stop.ps1 files are added.
Key Insight: Windows batch files have poor integration with conda. For conda workflows on Windows, PowerShell is a better choice. Always test environment activation in a new shell, rather than using inherited conda sessions.
18. CalendarPro simulation patch fails because generate_with_fallback is locally imported inside the method, not at the module level. Solution: The patch target is changed from ‘src.thoughts.thought_organizer.generate_with_fallback’ to ‘src.ai.provider_selector.generate_with_fallback’, so the patch can be applied at the source module level.
Key Insight: During simulation, patches should be placed where the function definition is, not where it is imported—local import creates new references, thereby bypassing the module-level patch.
19. After creating test_thoughts.py, CalendarPro pytest async tests fail due to the ‘coroutine never awaited’ warning. Solution: The pytest-asyncio package is installed, which can automatically detect async test functions and run them in the event loop.
Key Insight: pytest itself does not support async tests—pytest-asyncio plugin must be introduced as a dependency in pyproject.toml.
Comparison of Human and AI Approaches Strategic Level Root cause analysis method for demonstration replay Role Method Human Systematic three-layer analysis: (1) By comparing recorded code and replay code, environmental configuration mismatch is identified; (2) Secondary issues (initialization fluctuations, no proximity threshold) are recognized; (3) It is realized that the previous threshold increase is a cover for the real problem AI May continue adjusting proximity thresholds and detector parameters, only handling symptoms rather than identifying the misconfiguration causing the problem Detailed Requirements for the Plan Document Role Method Human Multiple times refusing ExitPlanMode, explicitly requesting “every sentence of the plan be written in the plan file” — emphasizing full self-containedness, including all exact line numbers and code snippets AI Initially wrote high-level steps and a file checklist, assuming exact line numbers and code can be found during implementation Difference Analysis: Humans emphasize future session recovery capability — the plan must be fully executable without current context. AI undervalues the importance of self-containedness and requires multiple iterations to understand expectations (the plan is a complete implementation manual, not a short task list).
Doubts about EEF distance calculation errors when the robot never approaches the object Role Method Human When informed that the robot never approached 0.22 meters, immediately question the distance measurement method, ask “how was it calculated?” and suspect measurement issues AI Initially accepted 0.22 meters as the true value, focusing on threshold adjustment (0.05→0.15→0.25→0.30 meters), rather than verifying the measurement itself Difference Analysis: Human domain knowledge (pick-and-place requires contact) triggers doubts about measurements. AI treats symptom (threshold adjustment) as a solution and only questions measurement validity after guidance.
Diagnosing faults from production logs Role Method Human Reading startup logs, immediately detecting SR/LLM mismatch (“leetcode” classified as manage_recurring) and calendar 403 errors, enabling root cause diagnosis without prompts AI Does not analyze logs actively. Requires human pointing out specific issues before investigation begins Difference Analysis: Humans conduct domain-aware log analysis (understanding intent classification semantics and error propagation patterns). AI only reacts to explicit instructions.
Implementation strategy and technical choices for MIHD improvement plan Role Method Human Choose “full sequential implementation from Phase 1 to Phase 7” (not partial), adopt a cyclic Q-Former version (no batch optimization), and batch corrections require multiple segments (not just one segment) AI Provides 3 options (complete/partial/specific phase), asks about performance optimization (Q-Former batch) and functionality scope (single mode vs. joint mode) for each technical decision point Difference Analysis: Humans prefer completeness and gradual optimization (first implement cyclic version, then consider batch), while AI offers options to balance performance. Human understanding of batch correction cases indicates no need for single-segment mode fixes
Concept of AI agent documentation Role Method Human Documentation should focus on non-obvious information: server limits, architecture patterns requiring multi-file understanding, common pitfalls. Remove discoverable information (file tree, method signatures) and duplicate content AI AI typically creates comprehensive reference documents containing full file trees, detailed API signatures, troubleshooting sections, and redundant content across chapters Difference Analysis: Humans realize AI agents can discover structure via tools without reference materials — context guidance is needed. AI defaults to providing comprehensive documentation suitable for human developers
Implementation planning and task decomposition for CalendarPro Role Method Human Provides extremely detailed plans, including exact file paths, method signatures, code examples, integration points, and reasons — minimizing ambiguity AI System executes plans, creates TodoWrite tasks, performs execution in dependency order, but occasionally needs trial-and-error for boundaries not covered by the plan (e.g., mock patch paths) Difference Analysis: Humans anticipate architecture and integration challenges in advance, while AI excels at system execution but requires iteration to discover uncovered boundaries
Two-stage export/merge workflow for multi-device summary | Role | Method | |——|——| | Human | Immediately realizes need for device-specific export, requiring centralized merge due to physical device separation and manual file transfer | | AI | Initially proposed a single-stage solution running on all devices simultaneously, ignoring actual constraints of offline device collaboration
Difference Analysis: Humans foresee operational constraints (manual file copying, asynchronous device usage), while AI did not consider these factors in design. User domain knowledge about real usage patterns drives architecture decisions
Autonomous agent for code repository exploration Role Method Human Explicitly starts 3 parallel exploration agents, fully understands CalendarPro’s vision, intelligence layer, and scalability before writing PLANNING.md AI Typically reads key files sequentially, gradually accumulating understanding — human method is more comprehensive and parallel Difference Analysis: Humans recognize the value of using professional agents for comprehensive early exploration, which is more strategic than typical incremental AI methods
AI Limitations Key Limitations Initially misdiagnosed visual issues as “frame missing”; real issue is “missing causal context” — failed to understand that error injection requires a narrative of timing (playback → trigger → injection) Cannot independently identify the root cause of playback — requires human analysis showing mismatch between PickPlace_D0+ controller configuration and pure PickPlace configuration. May continue parameter adjustments instead of questioning basic environment configuration Does not actively analyze production logs to identify vulnerabilities. Requires human diagnosis before implementing fixes (SR/LLM mismatch, error swallowing) Initially failed to understand the concept of “self-contained plan” — needed multiple rejections of ExitPlanMode before realizing all exploration results (exact line numbers, code snippets, file summaries) must be written in the plan file, not relying on external context Attempts to autonomously exit plan mode without clear user confirmation — failed to realize that comprehensive 3-agent exploration output requires human review before implementation General Limitations Failed to build SSH commands multiple times due to omitting “cd” to project directory (more than 6 times), even though user corrected it — failed to update understanding model of cluster file system structure Did not run validation tests before modifying MIHD GPU monitoring code. While the fix is correct (background thread sampling), lack of actual runtime validation Attempted cmd.exe conda solution before realizing platform limitations. Requires human guidance on using PowerShell as the correct solution During testing simulations, initially patched at the error module level (local import path instead of source module) — needs gradual correction through test execution Learning Outcomes Key Takeaways — Environment configuration (controller_configs) fundamentally changes robot dynamics in the robot suite. When replaying examples, always extract and use precise env_name + env_kwargs from HDF5 dataset metadata. Error injection visualization requires a three-stage narrative: (1) replay example actions that trigger; (2) moments showing detection triggers; (3) error injection and consequences. Static snapshot recovery loses the context of “why injection now”. Accuracy of robot simulation replay requires identical environment configuration and controller parameters (OSC_POSE, kp, damping coefficient, ramp_ratio), not just task name. Must load example metadata (env_args in HDF5) to reproduce the same dynamics. Never ignore errors (just print and return None). Must pass error messages along with context to the display layer. Users cannot fix errors they cannot see. Multi-device workflow uses a two-stage pattern: local export (no API required) + remote merge (requires API). Key elements include versioned intermediate formats (JSON logs), device information collection, optional per-device summaries. The goal of “planning mode” is to generate a fully self-contained implementation manual, requiring all exploration results (exact code location, line numbers, function signatures, existing code snippets), not a simple task list. Systematic root cause analysis is better than gradual parameter adjustment. When detection fails, systematically compare recording and playback environment configurations before adjusting thresholds. Parameter expansion often hides the underlying mismatch issue. When two classifiers have conflicting opinions (semantic router and LLM), trust the one with more context (LLM). Keyword matching fails in ambiguous expressions. Timeout protection requires dual defense: use asyncio.wait_for() for coroutine-level timeout, use httpx.Timeout() for connection-level timeout — different failure modes require different protection mechanisms. Production AI systems must not crash due to malformed AI output — implement three-stage fallback (direct parsing → fix → safe default) and log everything in each stage. When implementing new features in the existing code base, studying similar patterns (ThoughtOrganizer → PeriodicChecker) ensures architectural consistency and reduces integration resistance. Fault-tolerant design for spatial transcript data: multi-path candidates search (main_dir and Dataset/DLPFC), image processing boundary checks, statistical model fallback strategy (mclust → KMeans). MuJoCo cvel stores [angular(3), linear(3)], not [linear(3), angular(3)]. Always verify binary data layout against main documentation, not relying on inline comments. AI agent documentation should focus on non-obvious information and architecture patterns requiring multi-file understanding, not comprehensive reference materials. AI agents can discover file structure and method signatures via tools, but need context guidance on pitfalls and constraints. Google Calendar API’s periodic events: singleEvents=True returns instance ID, but update/delete operations require explicit field extraction (recurrence, recurringEventId) to avoid global changes. Comprehensive planning document (including maturity rating, roadmap priority, architecture rationale in PLANNING.md) provides strategic foundation for gradual development. Asyncio background tasks need clear lifecycle management: use create_task + done_callback for monitoring, close() for cleanup, proper exception logging to prevent silent failures. CalendarPro architecture pattern: JSONL appends to speed up (thoughts.jsonl, intent_mismatches.jsonl), JSON for mutable state, reuse existing data sources (DEFAULT_MEALS/DEFAULT_SLEEP) as a single real source. Comprehensive preliminary exploration (using parallel Explore agents) before writing architecture documentation is more effective than gradual discovery — strategic thinking yields results. Two-stage pipeline (export→merge) is natural for multi-device workflows and suitable for manual data transfer. Local export supports incremental processing and asynchronous device usage. Lazy import (import statements inside methods) helps break circular dependencies, but requires special testing: simulate namespace of consumption module, not the original module. Practical Experience Automate data collection using existing tools (ccusage) instead of reimplementing. Design considerations: subprocess fault tolerance (silently skip on failure), multi-device aggregation strategy (summation/merge), readable display format (tables vs. lists). Use of Git submodule: suitable for independent remote subprojects, records commit hash not branch, clone requires –recursive, update requires cd + git pull + commit hash change. Monitoring peak statistics needs continuous sampling during runtime (background thread), not just startup/stop snapshots. Requires proper thread lifecycle management (Event mechanism) to avoid resource leaks. Windows conda workflow requires PowerShell, not cmd.exe. Batch files lack proper conda integration. Always test environment activation in a new shell. When simulating in pytest, always patch at the source module where the function is defined, not at import — local import creates new references, bypassing module-level patches. Cluster file system semantics: shared storage means identical paths between nodes, but SSH sessions default to home directory — must explicitly execute cd in remote commands. Learning Insights Architecture The correct layered architecture for public GitHub Pages submissions: public users → relay (validation/throttling/ masking) → repository_dispatch → queue file → daily batch processing (duplication/cleaning/append CSV) → commit/push → automatic Pages deployment. The relay layer is a key isolation layer that protects repository write permissions. Semantic consistency between interface names and actual behavior must be strict: the name ‘staig_fusion’ naturally promises the same meaning as STAIG; allowing significant differences in default behavior can cause many hidden errors; global coverage behaviors (e.g., forcing encoder to UNI) must be clearly indicated in logs. Debugging Plotly 6.x defaults to binary-encoded arrays for serialization, causing bar length parsing errors when incompatible with older CDN. Solution: Strictly lock the CDN version to match the Python package version, force input as a Python list instead of pandas Series. Low CPU and GPU utilization simultaneously indicates the program is waiting on single-thread I/O, not CPU; performance bottlenecks in visual feature extraction usually occur in data preprocessing (patch extraction) rather than model forward pass. Errors in R interfaces (e.g., mclust) are not intuitive in Python; sufficient pre-validation should be added at the Python level and clear error messages with shape information provided; when R packages are unavailable, silent degradation must be clearly warned against, and algorithm behavior should not be changed without notice. Domain Knowledge There are five quantifiable key implementation differences between MIHD and original STAIG (prioritized): ① Mixed coordinate scales for full-resolution images (most critical); ② Silent degradation of mclust; ③ Reversed gene preprocessing order; ④ Difference in number of pseudo-label clusters; ⑤ Hyperparameter and image transform differences. The ARI gap (0.21→0.56) is mainly determined by ①②③. AI Usage Notes Effective Modes:
✓ Systematic cross-repo code comparison: comparing two code bases line by line, quantifying and identifying multiple implementation differences, and prioritizing them. ✓ Multiple tool calls combined with human observation: AI detects technical details (coordinate scales), user observes encoder coverage issues (runtime), creating a complementary approach. ✓ Architecture design supplementation: humans propose core security intuitions (confirmation before upload, secure isolation), AI translates them into complete executable technical architectures. Limitations:
✗ Insufficient thoroughness in fixes: when removing trend charts, only the call was removed initially, and a second fix is needed. ✗ Easy to overlook existing global coverage logic: when adding UNI2 tqdm, not realizing that strict mode will force encoder coverage. ✗ No pre-check of HPC environment modules (e.g., scanpy) before verification, leading to ModuleNotFoundError during validation, increasing debugging rounds. ✗ Multiple options for low GPU utilization issues, but no active suggestion to use profile tools (py-spy, nvprof) to precisely locate the actual bottleneck. Next Week Outlook The highest priority next week is verifying the runtime effect of strict STAIG alignment modification: ① Fix the mixed coordinate scales issue (full-resolution images should not multiply by the hires scaling factor), which is the most critical step for ARI improvement; ② Confirm the upstream root cause of mclust dimension is zero and fix it; ③ Install rpy2 and R mclust packages to eliminate the silent degradation risk in HPC environment. For the benchmark tool, GPU utilization optimization can be selectively promoted (DataLoader multi-process or patch cache pre-extraction scheme). English learning will continue focusing on grammar weaknesses such as subject-verb agreement.

Daily Report — 2026-02-01 Overview of Daily Work Completed Work: Resolved the unexpected drop in clustering metrics in MIHD benchmarks (ARI decreased from about 0.4 to about 0.13), aligned GCN implementation with the original STAIG framework, and verified a new GCN+UNI2+STAIG_fusion configuration. Implementation Steps: Identified environment mismatches and parameter drift by comparing git history and experiment logs; restored the benchmark conda environment (General); fixed STAIGTrainer.py and run_benchmark_core.py; updated GCNGeneEncoder to apply activation functions on all layers including the final projection layer. Impact: Restored clustering performance in benchmarks to expected levels (ARI >0.45), eliminated architectural drift between MIHD and STAIG codebases, and established a reliable configuration propagation scheme for future multimodal fusion experiments. By correcting environment dependencies, re-aligning default hyperparameters with the original STAIG architecture, and fixing graph convolutional activation logic, the critical benchmark accuracy drop in MIHD spatial transcriptomics workflows was resolved.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ Resolved ARI drop in MIHD benchmarks — Identified root causes including environment mismatches (base and General), drifting training hyperparameters, and incorrect original gene expression bypassing; restored benchmark configuration and verified metric recovery. ✅ Aligned MIHD GCN architecture with STAIG — Detected differences in activation function application in GCNGeneEncoder; fixed forward propagation to match hierarchical activation in original STAIG, and recorded architectural differences across projects. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Tested GCN + UNI2 + STAIG_fusion configuration — Configured the benchmark runner to support --gene_encoder gcn; executed test suite, fixed dependency issues (torch_geometric, scikit-misc), and successfully generated visualizations and embeddings. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Despite no major functional changes, benchmark ARI dropped from about 0.4+ to about 0.13. Solution: Identified incorrect conda environment execution and drifting default settings in STAIGTrainer.py; fallback to tau, num_epochs and edge weight methods (softmax_neglog -> softmax_log) to verify benchmark values.
Key Insight: In multimodal training comparisons, minor parameter drift (temperature scaling, iteration count) and environmental dependency mismatches severely disrupt convergence and clustering boundaries.
2. Previous workflow updates caused STAIG fusion failures by injecting original 3000-dimensional gene expression instead of precomputed 50-dimensional PCA embeddings. Solution: Removed raw_gene_expr’s bypass logic in run_benchmark_core.py; restored the correct low-dimensional embedding workflow to match the original STAIG training dynamics.
Key Insight: Hybrid models with internal GCN layers require strict input dimension alignment; bypassing precomputed embeddings for raw data fundamentally changes graph topology and destroys comparison targets.
3. GCNGeneEncoder of MIHD omits activation functions in the final layer, which does not conform to the original STAIG specification. Solution: Updated GCNGeneEncoder.forward() to apply activation functions by default on all layers; added configurable parameter apply_activation_to_last_layer=True to support older versions.
Key Insight: Applying nonlinear functions in the final projection layer of channel-expanded GCN significantly alters the feature space geometry; thus strict architectural replication is crucial for reproducibility.
Human and AI Approaches Strategic Level Identification of Root Causes of ARI Drop Role Method Human Analyzed git diffs, compared early successful and failed experiment logs, and quickly determined that environment (rpy2 dependencies) and configuration drift were the main issues. AI Initially relied on iterative execution and diff analysis; the human identified environmental mismatches and referenced historical benchmark states to validate post-fix adjustments. Analysis Difference: Humans drove theoretical alignment based on mathematical implementation standards. AI efficiently performs structural fixes and abstracts actual differences (e.g., O(n^2) vs. KD-tree graph construction) into operable documentation.
AI Limitations Key Limitations Initially failed to directly link code execution failures to environmental dependencies (rpy2/conda mismatch), requiring human intervention to determine the correct running context. General Limitations Iterative bash trial-and-error methods introduced delay; earlier static analysis of git blame or configuration propagation paths would be more beneficial for faster detection of parameter drift. Lessons Learned Key Experiences In multimodal fusion benchmarks, switching clustering backends (e.g., R’s mclust vs. Python’s kmeans) without considering algorithmic differences may artificially lower metric scores, even if the coding pipeline is functionally correct. Configuration-based training loops heavily rely on explicit parameter inheritance; implicit discarding of yaml values during nested object initialization leads to hard-to-trace performance degradation unless strict diff audits are performed. Today’s problem 3432. Count Partitions with Even Sum Difference
Intuition In this question, we need to partition the array into two parts. And the difference between these two parts are even.
Now, both parts must have the same module to 2. That is, they are both even or both odd. So, the sum of the array needs to be even.
Now, if the sum of the array is even, then every partition must have the same module to 2. Otherwise, the sum of the array would be odd.
Therefore, the answer would be 0 when the sum of the array is odd, and $n-1$ when the sum of the array is even.
Approach Return 0 when the sum of the array is odd, and $n-1$ when the sum of the array is even.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(n)$, n is the length of the array.
Space complexity: $O(n)$, n is the length of the array.
Code class Solution: def countPartitions(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: if sum(nums) % 2 == 1: return 0 return len(nums) - 1
summary: 1. Count Partitions with Even Sum Difference

content:
Question Burst Balloons
Intuition While the ballons burst, it will not affect the score of another ballon, and the length of the list will always decrease. This means that we can use dynamic programming to solve this problem.
Approach Consider a case, when $dp[i][j]$ means the maximum score you can get by bursting all the balloons between i and j. In this case, our answer would be $dp[0][n-1]$, if n is the length of the list.
Now, let’s figure out how to get $dp[i][j]$. As we mentioned in part Intuition, the length of the balloon is always decreasing, which means that we might be able to get $dp[i][j]$ by first counting a shorter interval, and the increase the interval to $0 \to n-1$.
Now, we have our solution:
First, we iterate the length of the interval.
Next, we can break the interval $i \to j$ into two sub intervals $i \to k-1$ and $k+1 \to j$.
Now we can compute the score of interval $i \to j$ by adding up sub intervals $i \to k-1$, $k + 1 \to j$, and burst the balloon k.
Because the balloons in sub interval $i \to k-1$ and $k + 1 \to j$ are already gone, so the score addition would be $nums[k] \times nums[i-1] \times nums[j+1]$.
The only thing we now need to consider is the edge of these subintervals. Knowing that the balloon we are now bursting can be the edge of the interval $i \to j$, meaning that we need to iterate $[i, j]$ inclusively.
Finally, you will get your result in $dp[0][n-1]$.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N^3)$. N is the length of the list. Space complexity: $O(N^2)$. N is the length of the list. Code class Solution: def maxCoins(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: n = len(nums) nums = nums + [1] dp = [[0 for _ in range(n+1)] for _ in range(n+1)] for i in range(n): dp[i][i] = nums[i] * nums[i-1] * nums[i+1] for i in range(1, n): for l in range(n): if i + l == n: break r = i + l for k in range(l, r+1): dp[l][r] = max(dp[l][r], dp[l][k-1] + dp[k+1][r] + nums[k] * nums[l-1] * nums[r + 1]) # print(dp) return dp[0][n-1]
summary: Interval Dynamic Programming with clear explaination and how you can get to the solution

Today’s problem 2894. Divisible and Non-divisible Sums Difference
Intuition We are given an integer n and a divisor m, and we want to compute the difference between:
The sum of numbers from 1 to n that are not divisible by m. The sum of numbers from 1 to n that are divisible by m. This means we want to partition the numbers 1 to n into two groups based on divisibility by m, sum each group, and return the difference.
Approach We can solve this problem using two methods:
Method 1: Formula-Based Use the formula for the sum of the first n natural numbers: n * (n + 1) // 2 to get the total sum. Count how many numbers from 1 to n are divisible by m: k = n // m. The divisible numbers are: m, 2m, ..., km, and their sum is m * (1 + 2 + ... + k) = m * (k * (k + 1) // 2). Subtract the divisible sum from the total to get the sum of non-divisible numbers, then subtract. Method 2: Brute-Force Iteration Iterate from 1 to n. If the number is divisible by m, add it to num2. Otherwise, add it to num1. Return the difference num1 - num2. Complexity Time complexity:
Method 1: $O(1)$ (constant time using formulas) Method 2: $O(n)$ (linear time iteration) Space complexity:
Both methods: $O(1)$ (only a few variables used) Code class Solution: def differenceOfSums(self, n: int, m: int) -> int: # Method 1: Formula-Based total_sum = n * (n + 1) // 2 k = n // m divisible_sum = m * (k * (k + 1) // 2) return total_sum - divisible_sum class Solution: def differenceOfSums(self, n: int, m: int) -> int: # Method 2: Brute-Force Iteration num1, num2 = 0, 0 for i in range(1, n + 1): if i % m == 0: num2 += i else: num1 += i return num1 - num2 Advertisement For more solutions, please visit My blog

Today’s problem 2131. Longest Palindrome by Concatenating Two Letter Words
Intuition There are in total two ways to form a palindrome.
a string that has an inverse string in the list a string that is a palindrome itself. In this case, the string that is palindrome can only exisit in the middle of the palindrome. Approach Therefore, we can use a hash to solve this problem. Note that we will first run test 1 before test 2. If there is an inverse string in the list, then put that string and the current string into the list.
Then test whether this string is a palindrome itself.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of words.
Space complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of words.
Code class Solution: def longestPalindrome(self, words: List[str]) -> int: cnt = Counter(words) ans = 0 sp = 0 for word, t in cnt.items(): # print(word, t) if word[0] == word[1]: ans += (t - t % 2) sp |= (t % 2) else: ans += min(t, cnt[word[::-1]]) return (ans + sp) * 2 Advertisement For more solutions, please visit My blog
summary: Hash!

content:
Today’s problem 3068. Find the Maximum Sum of Node Values
Important: all the methods below are based on this fact: xor even times equals xor zero times. Method 1: Tree DP Intuition and Approach In this problem, if we only consider one direction, e.g., from root to leaf, then the process will not have after effect (later decisions will not affect previous ones). Therefore, we can use DP to solve this problem.
The hardest part is the definition of the dp. As we have a prerequisite of a direction, a better way to define the dp formula is to exclude the effect of current node. Also, for each node, there are two status, as described above, each node can either xor odd times or even times.
Therefore, we have our DP definition. $dp[x][0/1]$ means the largest value the children of x can achieve when the node x is changed (1) or unchanged (0).
Now, for each child c of node x, we can do two operations: either do xor for both node x and c, or do not do xor for neither x nor c.
The dp formula of these two operations will be: (Note: the priority of $\oplus$ is lower than $+$, so it is very important to add a parentheses.)
Do the xor operation $dp[x][0] = max(dp[x][0] + dp[c][0] + nums[c], dp[x][0] + dp[c][1] + (nums[c] \oplus k))$. $dp[x][1] = max(dp[x][1] + dp[c][0] + nums[c], dp[x][1] + dp[c][1] + (nums[c] \oplus k))$. NOT do the xor operation $dp[x][0] = max(dp[x][1] + dp[c][1] + nums[c], dp[x][1] + dp[c][0] + (nums[c] \oplus k))$. $dp[x][1] = max(dp[x][0] + dp[c][0] + nums[c], dp[x][0] + dp[c][0] + (nums[c] \oplus k))$. Note that the dp[x][0] and dp[x][1] should be renewed at the same time.
Moreover, another important thing is the initialization of the dp array. For all $dp[x][1]$, we will give it a value of $-inf$, so that we can avoid the case when c is a leaf node and the number is $\oplus$ with k contributes to the $dp[x]$ array.
The final result will be $max((dp[0][0] + nums[0]), (dp[0][1] + (nums[0] ^ k)))$
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Space complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Code class Solution: def maximumValueSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: n = len(nums) dp = [[0 for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(n)] for i in range(n): dp[i][1] = -10_000_000_000 edge = [[] for _ in range(n)] for x,y in edges: edge[x].append(y) edge[y].append(x) def dfs(x, fa): for to in edge[x]: if to == fa: continue dfs(to, x) c0 = max(dp[to][0] + nums[to], dp[to][1] + (nums[to] ^ k)) c1 = max(dp[to][0] + (nums[to] ^ k), dp[to][1] + nums[to]) dp[x][0], dp[x][1] = max(dp[x][0] + c0, dp[x][1] + c1), max(dp[x][1] + c0, dp[x][0] + c1) dfs(0,-1) return max((dp[0][0] + nums[0]), (dp[0][1] + (nums[0] ^ k))) Method 2: Tree DP with better memory Intuition and Approach In the previous code, we find that the $dp[x]$ will only use two times. Once in calculating the result of $dp[x]$, once in calculating the result of $dp[fa]$.
Therefore, we can return the value of $dp[x][0]$ and $dp[x][1]$ to avoid the extra space of the dp array.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Space complexity: $O(1)$. Code class Solution: def maximumValueSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: n = len(nums) edge = [[] for _ in range(n)] for x,y in edges: edge[x].append(y) edge[y].append(x) def dfs(x, fa): dp0,dp1 = 0,-1e9 for to in edge[x]: if to == fa: continue c0, c1 = dfs(to, x) dp0, dp1 = max(dp0 + c0, dp1 + c1), max(dp0 + c1, dp1 + c0) return max(dp0 + nums[x], dp1 + (nums[x] ^ k)), max(dp0 + (nums[x] ^ k), dp1 + nums[x]) return dfs(0,-1)[0] Important: all the methods below are based on this fact: there are always a path between two nodes on a tree. Therefore, we can $\oplus$ all the nodes on this path, resulting the $\oplus$ of any two nodes on the tree. Method 3: DP without tree Intuition and Approach For each node, we have two status, whether to $\oplus$ k or not. Therefore, the definition of the DP array will be: $dp[i][0/1]$ means whether there are odd (1) or even (0) $\oplus$ k operations when traversing to the ith node.
We then have the formular:
When this node $\oplus$ with k: $dp[i][0] = max(dp[i-1][0] + nums[i], dp[i-1][1] + (nums[i] ^ k))$ When this node do not $\oplus$ with k: $dp[i][1] = max(dp[i-1][1] + nums[i], dp[i-1][0] + (nums[i] ^ k))$ Note that there are always even $\oplus$ operations, so the answer would be $dp[n-1][0]$.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Space complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Code class Solution: def maximumValueSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: n = len(nums) dp = [[0 for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(n)] dp[0][0] = nums[0] dp[0][1] = (nums[0] ^ k) for i in range(1, n): dp[i][0] = max(dp[i-1][0] + nums[i], dp[i-1][1] + (nums[i] ^ k)) dp[i][1] = max(dp[i-1][0] + (nums[i] ^ k), dp[i-1][1] + nums[i]) return dp[-1][0] Method 4: DP without tree with better memory Intuition and Approach Same as Method 2, we also find out that the dp[i] formular only use twice. In this case, we can use two variables instead of the whold array to have a better memory usage.
Also, the $max$ operations is too slow in python, so a better way is to use if else equations instead of max.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Space complexity: $O(1)$. Code class Solution: def maximumValueSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: n = len(nums) dp0, dp1 = 0, -10_000_000_000 for i in range(n): a = nums[i] b = a ^ k new_dp0 = dp0 + a if dp0 + a > dp1 + b else dp1 + b new_dp1 = dp0 + b if dp0 + b > dp1 + a else dp1 + a dp0, dp1 = new_dp0, new_dp1 return dp0 Method 5: Greedy algorithm Intuition and Approach Another way to look at this method without of tree is using greedy algorithm. Because we know that we can $\oplus$ k as long as we can find a pair of nodes, we can use greedy algorithm to find the pairs that has the most differences after $\oplus$ k.
That is, we can first $\oplus$ every element with k, calculating the difference between the new array and the previous array, then find all the pairs that has a difference that is larger than zero, then we get our answer.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Space complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of nums. Code class Solution: def maximumValueSum(self, nums: List[int], k: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: ans = sum(nums) diff = [(x ^ k) - x for x in nums] cnt,l,r = 0,inf,-inf for x in diff: if x > 0: cnt += 1 if x < l: l = x ans += x else: if r < x: r = x if cnt % 2 == 1: ans += max(-l, r) return ans I don’t know why using sort to do greedy algorithm is so neat and fast. Just as the one in the official solution.

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/zero-array-transformation-iii/
Intuition This question requires us to find the number of sections that is “useful”, or in other words, the smallest number of sections that is enough to make the array a zero array.
The key to solve this question is to change a view of how we look at this problem: if we take each element in the array seperately, then we can use greedy algorithm to solve this problem.
The thing is, if we look at each element seperately, i.e., to make the entire array a zero array, we must make each element zero.
In this case, for each element, the best way is to find a section that contains this elemnt, while it has a further tail. This is because a furtuer tail means to cover more elements in the future, which will be always better compared with the sections that has a shorter tail.
Therefore, now we need a data structure to store the current “farest tail”. This data structure need to add element dynamically and delete the largest item, when a heap will be the best way to store the “tail”.
Approach Therefore, we can form our algorithm.
First, we need to sort the array using the left end of the query as keyword. In this case, we can find which queries has a left end that is to the left of our current index. Then we need to create a difference array to deal with the section add operation; a heap to store the right end of the queries; and an index to show where we are currently at when we traverse all the queries. The next step is to traverse the number array: for each element in the number array, we first need to push all the queries that has the left end that is less the current index. This makes all the elements in the heap potentially available to use to decrease the current element. Then we will deal with the current element, finding all the available queries for the current element, then deal with the section decrease operation. (In this case, we ensure every operation is valid by checking that the endpoint of the heap top is larger or equal to the index, so that the left end of the array will be less or equal to the current index, and the right end of the array will be larger or equal to the current index. Therefore, we guarentee that the operation is valid). Finally, if the number is still larger than 0, we will return -1; otherwise, we will return the remaining element in h, which is all the unused elements. Complexity Time complexity: $O(N \times log(m))$
Space complexity: $O(N + M)$
Code class Solution: def maxRemoval(self, nums: List[int], queries: List[List[int]]) -> int: queries.sort(key = lambda x: x[0]) diff = [0] * (len(nums) + 1) h = [] idx, now = 0,0 for i in range(len(nums)): while idx < len(queries) and queries[idx][0] <= i: heappush(h, -queries[idx][1]) idx += 1 now += diff[i] while h and now < nums[i] and -h[0] >= i: now += 1 diff[-heappop(h) + 1] -= 1 if now < nums[i]: return -1 return len(h) For more solutions, please visit My blog
summary: Greedy Algorithm, look at each element seperately!

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/construct-smallest-number-from-di-string/
Intuition This problem let us find a sequence of numbers under some constrains.
First we observe that the N, the length of the sequence, is very small. Thereofre, we can use a dfs to traverse all possible situations and get the result.
Another way to do that is using a stack. When the array is increasing, the smallest way to get a valid array is to traverse all the numbers, filling in the smallest number possible. When the array is decreasing, becuase we still want the smallest array, we need to put the smallest number available, which should be also larger to the next number. In this case, the smallest number we can put at current place is the position + the number of consequtive ‘D’s afterward. Therefore, we can use a stack to temporarily sotre the number we are traversing, and add it back to the current array when we meet a ‘I’ or reach to the end of the array.
Approach For Solution 1, the dfs solution, all we need to do is to traverse all the solutions and get the first one that fullfills the requirement.
For Solution 2, the stack solution, when we meet ‘I’, we can put “idx + 1” to our current array, then fill all the elements in a stack into our current array in reverse order, then flush the stack. When we meet ‘D’, we can put “idx + 1” to our stack for our future use.
Trick DFS: Because we are required to find the smallest valid sequence, so the first sequence that is not None is our target. This means that we can return this answer as soon as we get a valid result.
Stack: Here I intentionally add a “D” to the end of the sequence. Intuitively speaking, the last element is the largest element in the sequence, so to put it into our current sequence, it requires a “D” operation. In this case, if the original last character is ‘I’, then we can directlly put the largest number to the end of our original sequence, which is the same as a ‘D’ operation. This is because the ‘I’ operation will flush the stack, so there will only be one element in the stack, making it the same whether adding as a normal sequence or a inverted sequence. If the original last character is ‘D’, then the largest character should be at the position whether the consequtive sequence of ‘D’ starts. In this case, this means that there should be a ‘D’ operation to put this number into the right position. Though this trick makes the code more tidy and elegant, it sacrifices readability, which is not encouraged.
Complexity Time complexity for dfs solution: $O(N!)$, N is the length of the sequence.
Time complexity for stack solution: $O(N)$, N is the length of the sequence.
Space complexity for dfs solution: $O(N)$, N is the length of the sequence.
Space complexity for stack solution: $O(N)$, N is the length of the sequence.
Code class Solution: def smallestNumber(self, pattern: str) -> str: arr = [] n = len(pattern) + 2 def dfs(arr): if len(arr) == n - 1: return arr now = len(arr) - 1 res = None if pattern[now] == 'I': for i in range(arr[now] + 1, n): if i not in arr: res = dfs(arr + [i]) if res is not None: return res else: for i in range(1, arr[now]): if i not in arr: res = dfs(arr + [i]) if res is not None: return res return res for i in range(1, n): ans = dfs([i]) if ans is not None: return ''.join(map(str, ans)) # return ans return None class Solution: def smallestNumber(self, pattern: str) -> str: arr = [] n = len(pattern) + 2 def dfs(arr): if len(arr) == n - 1: return arr now = len(arr) - 1 res = None if pattern[now] == 'I': for i in range(arr[now] + 1, n): if i not in arr: res = dfs(arr + [i]) if res is not None: return res else: for i in range(1, arr[now]): if i not in arr: res = dfs(arr + [i]) if res is not None: return res return res for i in range(1, n): ans = dfs([i]) if ans is not None: return ''.join(map(str, ans)) # return ans return None For more solutions, please visit My blog.

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/zero-array-transformation-i/
Intuition This problem means to decrease one in a range (l, r) for each query. To deal with the change of a range, we can consider prefix sum. Note that the question says “Select a subset of indices”, this means that we do not necessarily need to minus 1 for all indices in the range. In this case, because we only care whether the final array is a zero array or not, so instead of testing whether the final array is zero or not, we can test whether the final array is less or equal to zero or not becuase of the subset mentioned in the question.
Approach For each query, we can add 1 to the difference array at l and add -1 to the difference array at r + 1. Then when we calculate the final answer, we can use the prefix sum to add them up and get the change of the array. Finally, when we want to know whether the final array is zero array or not, we can add the difference array to the original array and test whether each index is less or equal to zero or not to get the answer.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N + M)$, N is the length of the original array, M is the length of the query.
Space complexity: $O(N)$.
Code class Solution: def isZeroArray(self, nums: List[int], queries: List[List[int]]) -> bool: diff = [0] * (len(nums) + 1) for l, r in queries: diff[l] -= 1 diff[r + 1] += 1 for i in range(len(nums)): if i > 0: diff[i] += diff[i-1] if nums[i] + diff[i] > 0: # print(i, nums[i], diff[i]) return False return True For more solutions, please visit My blog

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/painting-a-grid-with-three-different-colors/
Intuition In this question, we find that m is relatively small compared with n. As $m \le 5$, and $n \le 1000$. Then we may consider to enumerate all solutions for a column, then elaborate it to the whole matrix. When elaborating it to the whole matrix, we figure out a thing: whatever a column is painted, the only influence is its next column, while future columns will not influence previous columns. This makes DP possible.
Approach Therefore, here is our approach:
First, we need to find out how many valid patterns are there in a column. Therefore, we can perform a dfs to search for all possible combinations. Second, we need to know which two patterns can be in adjcent columns, so we enumerate through each pair of patterns, and then test whether they can be in adjcent rows or not. Third, we use DP to elaborate from one column to the next. In this case, the DP formular will be: $DP[col][case_x] = \sum DP[col-1][case_y]. \forall \text{casex and casey can be in two adjcent columns}$. Finally, all we need to do is to add up all the cases of the final column of DP to get our answer. Complexity Time complexity: $O(3^{2m} \times n)$
Space complexity: $O(3^{2m})$
Code class Solution: def colorTheGrid(self, m: int, n: int) -> int: pat = [] col = [0, 1, 2] def dfs(x, s): if x == m: pat.append(s) return for i in col: if x == 0 or s[x - 1] != i: dfs(x + 1, s + [i]) dfs(0, []) # till this step, we find all valid patterns for a column and store it in the pattern list. l = len(pat) valid = [[True for _ in range(l)] for _ in range(l)] for i in range(l): for j in range(i + 1, l): for k in range(m): if pat[i][k] == pat[j][k]: valid[i][j] = False break # till this step, we find all the pattern pairs that is valid. dp = [[0 for _ in range(l)] for _ in range(n)] mod = 1_000_000_007 for i in range(l): dp[0][i] = 1 # for column 0, each pattern is valid. for i in range(1, n): for x in range(l): for y in range(x + 1, l): if valid[x][y]: dp[i][x] = (dp[i][x] + dp[i-1][y]) % mod dp[i][y] = (dp[i][y] + dp[i-1][x]) % mod # we elaborate to the next column according to the DP formula. ans = 0 for i in range(l): ans = (ans + dp[-1][i]) % mod # finally, we add up all the answers. return ans
summary: First DFS then DP!

今日问题 https://leetcode.com/problems/construct-the-lexicographically-largest-valid-sequence/description/
直觉分析 此问题要求你根据给定条件找到解决方案。
解决方法 注意 $N \le 20$，因此可以使用暴力搜索来寻找答案。
复杂度分析 时间复杂度：$O(N^N)$，其中 N 与问题定义中的数值相同。 空间复杂度：$O(N)$，其中 N 与问题定义中的数值相同。 代码实现 普通深度优先搜索解法 class Solution: def dfs(self, pos, n, vis, pls): if pos == 2 * n - 1: return pls # if we enumerate to the end of the sequence, then we can return the answer. if pls[pos] != 0: return self.dfs(pos + 1, n, vis, pls) # if we place a number in the current position, then we can move to the next position. for i in range(n, 1, -1): # we enumerate from large to small so that we can get the largest sequence. if vis[i]: continue # if we use this number, then pass. if pos + i < 2 * n - 1 and pls[pos + i] == 0: pls[pos] = i pls[pos + i] = i vis[i] = True # put the number into the slot if it is available. ret = self.dfs(pos + 1, n, vis, pls) if ret is not None: return ret vis[i] = False pls[pos] = 0 pls[pos + i] = 0 if vis[1]: return None vis[1] = True pls[pos] = 1 ret = self.dfs(pos + 1, n, vis, pls) if ret is not None: return ret vis[1] = False pls[pos] = 0 # special check for 1 becuase 1 only puts into one slot. return None def constructDistancedSequence(self, n: int) -> List[int]: pls = [0] * (2 * n - 1) # pls is the sequence that we place numbers vis = [0] * (n+1) # visit is the sequence we test whether a number exists in the current sequence or not. return self.dfs(0, n, vis, pls) 更高效的解决方案，便于后续使用 注意当输入相同数值时，解决方案不会改变，因此我们可以存储得到的答案，并用于每次查询。

Intuition In this question, we find that if we flip a coin twice, then it is the same as flipping it zero times. Moreover, the only three ways to flip a coin is: Flip this coin Flip the coin before Flip the coin before this coin This means that if we pass this coin, we can no longer flip this coin. Approach In this case, we can iterate from front to end and flip every coin that is 0, and check whether the whole array is 1 at the end. Why is this method correct then? First we know that we cannot flip a coin after we pass this coin.
This means that we must flip this coin. If we do not flip this coin, then this coin will remain 0, which does not satisfy the quetion. Therefore, this step is required, missing this step will not give us the array we need.
We can also prove that this will lead us to the result for every array that can achieve this step. Because you have to flip this coin no matter what operation you did.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$, N is the length of the array. Space complexity: $O(1)$. Code class Solution: def minOperations(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: cnt = 0 for i in range(len(nums) - 2): if nums[i] == 0: cnt += 1 nums[i] = 1 nums[i + 1] = 1 - nums[i + 1] nums[i + 2] = 1 - nums[i + 2] if nums[-1] == 1 and nums[-2] == 1: return cnt return -1

Intuition Situation 1: if there is no 0: In this case, we can just use a prefix multiplication to do what the question asks. Situation 2: if there is 0: Then it would be 0! Therefore, all we need is to just check whether there is a 0 in the last k numbers of the stream. If yes, them just return 0.

Code class ProductOfNumbers: def __init__(self): self.q = [] self.mul = 1 def add(self, num: int) -> None: self.mul *= num self.q.append(self.mul) if num == 0: self.q = [] self.mul = 1 def getProduct(self, k: int) -> int: if k > len(self.q): return 0 if k == len(self.q): return self.mul return self.mul // self.q[-k - 1] # Your ProductOfNumbers object will be instantiated and called as such: # obj = ProductOfNumbers() # obj.add(num) # param_2 = obj.getProduct(k)

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-operations-to-exceed-threshold-value-ii/description
Intuition Do what the question ask using heap.
Approach Get the minimum two from the list using heap. Put back value $2 * min(x, y) + max(x, y)$ to the heap. If the value you get is all larger or equal to k, then it is all done. Complexity Time complexity: $O(N\times log(N))$, N is the length of the sequence.
Space complexity: $O(1)$, by using heapify, there is no external storage.
Code class Solution: def minOperations(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int: ans = 0 heapify(nums) x = heappop(nums) while(len(nums) > 0 and x < k): y = heappop(nums) nx = min(x, y) * 2 + max(x, y) heappush(nums, nx) x = heappop(nums) ans += 1 return ans

Intuition In this question, we can simulate the process described in the question, and then get the answer.
Approach First write a count function that counts the sum of every integer. Use a dictionary to store the top two values. Compare the current number with two numbers stored in the dictionary. Code class Solution: def maximumSum(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: def cnt(x): res = 0 while(x > 0): res += x % 10 x //= 10 return res dic = dict() ans = -1 for x in nums: nx = cnt(x) if nx in dic: if x > dic[nx][0]: dic[nx][1] = dic[nx][0] dic[nx][0] = x if dic[nx][1] > 0: ans = max(ans, dic[nx][0] + dic[nx][1]) elif x > dic[nx][1]: dic[nx][1] = x ans = max(ans, dic[nx][0] + dic[nx][1]) else: dic.update({nx: [x, 0]}) return ans

Intuition In this case, we need to delete all the occurance of “part” in “s”. Therefore, we can check whether “s” contains “part”. Then we can delete it from the string.

Intuition In this question, we find that we need to find the pairs that has the same distance as the difference of nums.
In this case, if we distract the distance between these two numbers, then they would be the same.
That is: $j - i = nums[j] - nums[i] \Longrightarrow nums[j] - j = nums[i] = i$.
Then the question would be easy: we just subtract the index of every number in the list, and then found how many pairs of i,j in the nums array that has the same number.
We then subtract these counts from the total counts of answer.
Approach Count all pairs of i,j; that is, $N \times (N - 1)$, N is the length of the array. Subtract all the nums[i] by i. Count how many pairs of i,j has the same number. Subtract these i,j pairs from the original answer. Complexity Time complexity: $O(N)$. N is the length of the array.
Space complexity: $O(N)$. N is the length of the array.
Code class Solution: def countBadPairs(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: nums = [nums[i] - i for i in range(len(nums))] cnt = Counter(nums) N = len(nums) ans = N * (N - 1) // 2 for v in cnt.values(): ans -= v * (v - 1) // 2 return ans

Intuition In this question, we need to find the smallest index of the number in the list. Note that the index may change when dealing with the list. Because we need the smallest index, so we need a sorted datastructure. Trick: We can get a lazy tag that stores the number of each index, so that we can pop only when we find our current answer does not fullfill the requirement.

Code class NumberContainers: def __init__(self): self.lst = dict() self.idx = dict() def change(self, index: int, number: int) -> None: if number not in self.lst: self.lst.update({number: []}) heappush(self.lst[number], index) self.idx.update({index: number}) def find(self, number: int) -> int: if number not in self.lst: return -1 while self.lst[number]: currIndex = self.lst[number][0] if self.idx[currIndex] != number: heappop(self.lst[number]) else: return currIndex return -1 # Your NumberContainers object will be instantiated and called as such: # obj = NumberContainers() # obj.change(index,number) # param_2 = obj.find(number)

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/tuple-with-same-product/description/
Intuition In this question, all we need to do is to find the tuple that the numbers in the tuple has the same multiplication value. For example, if there are n pairs of numbers that has the same multiplication value, then the result would be $(^2_n) \times 4$. This is because we can pick any two pair from the set and form a tuple.
The question was, why can you prove that this two pairs are distinct?
This is because the original array is distinct. This means that there are no duplicated numbers in the original array. Therefore, if $a \times b = c \times d$, we know that $a \ne c$, then we can now that $b \ne d$.
Approach Therefore, all we need to do is to iterate through the whole list and find all tuples that has the same multiplication.
Trick Among four dictionaries, defaultdict, Counter, dict, and {}, dict has the fastest speed.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N ^ 2)$, N is the length of the array.
Space complexity: $O(N)$, we need to store the whole array.
Code class Solution: def tupleSameProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int: nums.sort() cnt = dict() N = len(nums) for i in range(N): for j in range(i + 1, N): tmp = nums[i] * nums[j] if tmp not in cnt: cnt[tmp] = 1 else: cnt[tmp] += 1 ans = 0 for v in cnt.values(): ans += 4 * (v) * (v - 1) return ans

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/divide-nodes-into-the-maximum-number-of-groups/description/
Intuition The key of this question is $|y - x| = 1$. We know that for a step further, the parity must change. Therefore, when we encounter a case when the parity has a problem (for example, a loop with three nodes and three edges), we would return -1. Otherwise, all we can do is to iterate the starting point of the graph to find which point is the best starting point.
Therefore, we can have our approach:
We can use a dfs to find whether there is a parity issue or not. We can use a bfs to find the starting point. Questions: why using bfs to find the starting point?
This is because we need to add a point to the next group if it has an edge connecting the current point and the next point.
Approach We can use a dfs to find whether there is a parity issue or not. We can use a bfs to find the starting point. Complexity Time complexity: $O(N^2)$
Space complexity: $O(N^2)$
Code class Solution: def magnificentSets(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> int: vis = [0] * (n + 1) bvis = [0] * (n + 1) e = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)] for x,y in edges: e[x].append(y) e[y].append(x) ans = 0 clock = 0 def bfs(x): nonlocal clock clock += 1 bvis[x] = clock q = deque([(x,1)]) res = 1 while(len(q) > 0): now, dis = q.popleft() res = max(res, dis) for to in e[now]: if bvis[to] == clock: continue bvis[to] = clock q.append((to, dis + 1)) return res cur = 0 def dfs(x): nonlocal cur cur = max(cur, bfs(x)) # print(cur) tmp = 0 for to in e[x]: if vis[to] == 0: if vis[x] == 0: print("Warning!", x) vis[to] = -vis[x] tmp += dfs(to) else: if vis[to] != -vis[x]: return -1 return tmp for i in range(1, n + 1): if vis[i] == 0: cur = 0 vis[i] = 1 if dfs(i) < 0: return -1 # print("out: ", cur) ans += cur # print(bfs(5)) return ans

Today’s problem https://leetcode.com/problems/making-a-large-island/description/
Intuition In this problem, we need to flip a 0 into a one to calculate the largest connected block. Now, if we can calculate the size of the connected block in the 4 directions of a 0 in the grid, then we just need to add them up and we are all set.
Approach First we need to calculate the size of each connected block and give a label to each connected block so that we are not adding the same connected block twice.
Then we iterate all the 0, flip its result is the sum of the unique connected blocks around it in 4 directions.
Complexity Time complexity: $O(N^2)$
Space complexity: $O(N^2)$
Code class Solution: def largestIsland(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int: islandCount = [0,0] dx = [0,0,1,-1] dy = [1,-1,0,0] n = len(grid) m = len(grid[0]) def dfs(x, y, cnt): grid[x][y] = cnt islandCount[cnt] += 1 for i in range(4): nx = x + dx[i] ny = y + dy[i] if nx < 0 or ny < 0 or nx >= n or ny >= m or grid[nx][ny] != 1: continue dfs(nx, ny, cnt) cnt = 1 for i in range(len(grid)): for j in range(len(grid[0])): if grid[i][j] == 1: cnt += 1 islandCount.append(0) dfs(i, j, cnt) ans = max(islandCount) for i in range(len(grid)): for j in range(len(grid[0])): if grid[i][j] == 0: tmp = 1 vis = set([]) for k in range(4): nx = i + dx[k] ny = j + dy[k] if nx < 0 or ny < 0 or nx >= n or ny >= m or grid[nx][ny] in vis: continue tmp += islandCount[grid[nx][ny]] vis.add(grid[nx][ny]) ans = max(ans, tmp) return ans
